title: ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ: the complete 2026 guide
dek: One form unlocks all three of New Jersey's property tax relief programs for seniors. Here is who qualifies, how much you could get, and how the PAS-1 works. The 2025 deadline was November 2, 2026.
keyFacts: PAS-1 deadline for 2025 benefits was November 2, 2026
Seniors who own their homes are not filed automatically
ANCHOR: up to $1,500 for homeowners, $700 for renters 65+
Stay NJ brings total relief up to 50% of taxes, max $6,500
body:
If you own or rent a home in New Jersey and you are 65 or older, the state may send you thousands of dollars this year. The money comes from three programs: ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ. One form covers all three. It is called the PAS-1, and the deadline for 2025 benefits was November 2, 2026.

That date has passed. If you missed it, call the Property Tax Relief hotline at 1-888-238-1233 to ask about your options, and watch for the next application. Many seniors still think they were filed automatically. Most were not. This guide walks you through who qualifies, what each program pays, how they fit together and how to file without a hitch.

What are the three programs?

Each program does a different job. ANCHOR (Affordable New Jersey Communities for Homeowners and Renters) is a flat payment for homeowners and renters. Senior Freeze (the Property Tax Reimbursement program) pays back any increase in your property taxes since your base year. Stay NJ is the newest. It aims to cover half of a senior homeowner's property tax bill, after the other two are counted.

ProgramWho it helps2025 benefit (paid 2026 to 2027)
ANCHORHomeowners and rentersHomeowners: $1,500 (income up to $150,000) or $1,000 ($150,001 to $250,000). Renters: $450 under 65, $700 at 65 or older (income up to $150,000)
Senior FreezeHomeowners and mobile home owners 65+ or on Social Security disabilityYour current tax bill minus your base year bill
Stay NJHomeowners 65+ with income up to $200,000Tops your total up to 50% of your taxes, with a ceiling of $6,500, $5,000 or $4,000 depending on income
One form, three programs. The 2025 deadline was November 2, 2026.

Who qualifies?

ANCHOR

You must have owned or rented your main home in New Jersey on October 1, 2025. Homeowners need 2025 New Jersey gross income of $250,000 or less. Renters need $150,000 or less. Mobile home owners are treated as renters for ANCHOR. Senior homeowners no longer get the extra $250 they received last year, so the homeowner maximum is $1,500 at any age. Senior renters still get the higher $700 amount.

Senior Freeze

You must have been 65 or older by December 31, 2025, or receiving Social Security disability benefits. First time applicants generally must have owned and lived in the same New Jersey home since December 31, 2022. Your income must be $168,268 or less for 2024 and $172,475 or less for 2025. Senior Freeze counts some income that the regular state income tax ignores, including Social Security. So do not assume you qualify just because you passed the ANCHOR test.

The reimbursement equals the property taxes billed for the current year minus the taxes billed for your base year. If your taxes went up, you get the difference back. If they did not, you get nothing from this program. Mobile home owners can be reimbursed for increases in park site fees.

Stay NJ

You or your spouse must have been 65 or older during 2025. You must own your home, and your 2025 income must be $200,000 or less. Renters and mobile home owners are not eligible. The ceiling depends on income: $6,500 if your income is $100,000 or less, $5,000 from $100,001 to $150,000, and $4,000 from $150,001 to $200,000.

How do the three programs stack?

The state calculates them in order. ANCHOR comes first, then Senior Freeze. Stay NJ is figured last. Its goal is to bring your combined relief up to half of your property tax bill, but no higher than your income ceiling. If ANCHOR and Senior Freeze together already cover half your bill, Stay NJ adds nothing. You cannot simply add the three maximums together. Your total relief can never exceed the taxes you actually paid.

These hypothetical examples use round numbers to show the math. Your year end letter from the state will show your real figures.

Example 1: A widow in Toms River

Say you are 72, have owned your Ocean County home since 2010, and had income of about $48,000 in both 2024 and 2025. Your 2025 property taxes were $7,800, and your base year bill was $7,400. ANCHOR pays $1,500. Senior Freeze pays $400 (the $7,800 bill minus the $7,400 base). Half your taxes is $3,900, well under the $6,500 ceiling. Stay NJ fills the gap: $3,900 minus $1,900 equals $2,000. Total relief: $3,900.

Example 2: A couple in Cherry Hill

Say you are 68 and 70, bought your Camden County home in 2023, and earned $130,000 in 2025. Your taxes were $14,000. Because you have not owned the home since 2022, Senior Freeze does not apply yet. ANCHOR pays $1,500. Half your taxes would be $7,000, but your income puts your ceiling at $5,000. Stay NJ pays the difference: $3,500. Total relief: $5,000.

Example 3: A renter in Montclair

Say you are 80 and rent an apartment in Essex County, with income of $40,000. Stay NJ and Senior Freeze are for homeowners, so they do not apply. ANCHOR pays $700 because you are 65 or older. If you were not required to file a state income tax return, the state may add the $50 Property Tax Credit to that payment.

How do I file the PAS-1?

Seniors and people on Social Security or Railroad Retirement disability must file the PAS-1 themselves. The state does not file it for you, even if you received ANCHOR automatically in a past year. You can file online at propertytaxreliefapp.nj.gov or on paper.

Gather these documents first

  • Your 2024 and 2025 property tax bills, or the details from your tax collector. You need the county and municipality code, your block, lot and qualifier, and the tax amounts for both years.
  • Your 2024 and 2025 NJ-1040 income tax returns, if you filed them.
  • Your SSA-1099 forms showing total Social Security benefits (Box 5). The quickest way to get them is a my Social Security account at ssa.gov.
  • Records of other income such as Roth IRA distributions or a total and permanent disability pension received before it converted to a regular pension.
  • A photo ID if you file online. The online application asks you to verify your identity, so have a photo ID such as a driver's license, state ID or passport ready.

The PAS-1 asks for income in several pieces. It includes lines from your NJ-1040, qualified Roth distributions, certain disability pension amounts and your total Social Security. Check the PAS-1 instructions for which disability payments to include. If you did not have to file a state return, the PAS-1 instructions include worksheets to help you add up your income.

  1. Pull your papers together. Use the list above. Put both years of tax bills side by side.
  2. Choose online or paper. Online lets you pick direct deposit for ANCHOR. Paper filers receive paper checks only.
  3. Verify your identity. If the identity check gives you trouble, stop and ask for help instead of guessing.
  4. Fill in every section that applies. Answer the ownership and residency questions carefully. If you co-own the home, enter your ownership share.
  5. Submit and save a copy. Keep your confirmation number or a photocopy of the paper form.

Need a hand? Call the Property Tax Relief hotline at 1-888-238-1233 or the Senior Freeze information line at 1-800-882-6597. You can also book a telephone appointment or visit a Division of Taxation Regional Information Center. During filing season, many county offices on aging and libraries hold filing events. The statewide Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 can point you to one near you.

What mistakes cost people money?

  • Assuming you were filed automatically. The state auto-filed most homeowners under 65 and most renters. Seniors who own their homes were not included. If you are 65 or older and own, you must file.
  • Skipping a year. If you miss a Senior Freeze year, you lose your base year and the reimbursement can reset. If you missed a year, call the Senior Freeze line to ask whether you can still file for it.
  • Using the wrong income figure. ANCHOR uses New Jersey gross income. Senior Freeze and Stay NJ also count Social Security and other items. Fill in every income line the form asks for.
  • Entering only one year of tax information. Senior Freeze needs both 2024 and 2025 figures.
  • Leaving out your ownership share. If you own half the home with a sibling, your benefit is based on half the taxes.
  • Waiting until the last week. Identity checks, missing tax bills and busy phone lines all take time.
  • Answering a text or email that asks for your information. The state warns that scammers send fake rebate messages. Go directly to nj.gov. Our guide to common scams in New Jersey explains the warning signs.

What happens after I file, and when will I be paid?

The Division of Taxation reviews your application and may write to you if something is missing. Answer quickly, because a pending question holds up every payment. You can check your status on the state's property tax relief status page.

ProgramWhen payments go out for 2025 benefitsHow
Senior FreezeBegan July 15, 2026, for early filers. Later filers are paid after review.Check
ANCHORBegan September 15, 2026, on a rolling basis. Most are paid within 90 days of filing.Direct deposit (online filers who choose it) or check
Stay NJBy check. The state says the 2025 benefit will be paid in February and May 2027Check

The February and May 2027 Stay NJ installments are covered by the Fiscal Year 2027 state budget. The state says its maximum amounts assume no changes in the Fiscal Year 2028 budget. Every program here depends on money the Legislature sets aside each year.

Near the end of the cycle, the state sends a determination letter that lists your exact amount from each program. Keep it with your tax papers. If the state overpays you, it can ask for the extra back. If a check arrives that you know you should not have received, mail it to the New Jersey Division of Taxation, PO Box 266, Trenton, NJ 08695-0266.

Then mark your calendar for next year. You will need to file a new PAS-1 for 2026 benefits. Filing every year protects your Senior Freeze base year and keeps Stay NJ coming.

Property tax relief is one piece of a bigger picture. If money is tight, read our guides to help with prescriptions and bills and food and utility assistance. If you are thinking about whether to stay in your house long term, see aging in place in New Jersey.

You may also find our guide to benefits for older veterans helpful.

faq.q: I got ANCHOR automatically last year. Do I need to file?
faq.a: If you are 65 or older, or on Social Security or Railroad Retirement disability, yes. The state did not auto-file seniors. The deadline for 2025 benefits was November 2, 2026. If you missed it, call 1-888-238-1233.

faq.q: Can I get all three programs at once?
faq.a: Yes, if you qualify for each. ANCHOR is calculated first, then Senior Freeze. Stay NJ tops up the total to half your property taxes, up to a ceiling of $6,500, $5,000 or $4,000 depending on income.

faq.q: I rent. What can I get?
faq.a: Renters can get ANCHOR only: $700 if you were 65 or older in 2025 and $450 if younger, with income of $150,000 or less. Senior Freeze and Stay NJ are for homeowners.

faq.q: When will Stay NJ checks arrive?
faq.a: For 2025 benefits, Stay NJ is paid by check. The state says the 2025 benefit will be paid in February and May 2027.

faq.q: Who can help me fill out the form?
faq.a: Call the Property Tax Relief hotline at 1-888-238-1233 or the Senior Freeze line at 1-800-882-6597. Regional Information Centers and many county offices on aging also offer free help.

faq.q: What is the income limit for Senior Freeze in 2026?
faq.a: For 2025 benefits, your income must be $168,268 or less for 2024 and $172,475 or less for 2025. Senior Freeze counts Social Security and some other income that the state income tax ignores.

title: PAAD, Senior Gold and Medicare help: how NJ seniors save
dek: One New Jersey application can cut your prescription copays to $5, pay your Medicare premium and add $225 a year for utilities. Here is who qualifies in 2026.
keyFacts: PAAD: $5 generic, $7 brand for income under $54,943 single / $62,390 married
Senior Gold covers up to $10,000 above the PAAD limits
Medicare Savings Programs can pay the $202.90 Part B premium
HAAAD repays up to $500 per hearing aid for PAAD and Lifeline members
PAAD and NJSave hotline: 1-800-792-9745
body:
New Jersey has some of the most generous prescription and Medicare help in the country. Plenty of people who qualify never apply. Some assume their income is too high. Others think the paperwork will be a nightmare. In most cases, one application called NJSave covers everything.

This guide explains five programs that can lower what you pay for medicine, Medicare and utilities. It also shows how to apply once and get screened for all of them.

What help is available, and who is it for?

Here are the 2026 income limits at a glance. All of these programs are for New Jersey residents. The state programs (PAAD, Senior Gold and Lifeline) require you to be 65 or older, or 18 to 64 and receiving Social Security disability benefits.

ProgramWhat it does2026 income limit (single / married)
PAADPrescriptions for $5 generic, $7 brandUnder $54,943 / under $62,390
Senior GoldPrescriptions for $15 plus half the remaining cost$54,943 to $64,943 / $62,390 to $72,390
Lifeline$225 a year toward utility costsSame as PAAD
Medicare Savings ProgramsPays your Medicare Part B premium, and sometimes moreUp to $21,546 / $29,214 (QI level), with an asset limit
Extra HelpLowers Part D premiums and drug copaysAbout $1,995 a month / $2,705 a month, with an asset limit

How do PAAD and Senior Gold work?

PAAD

Pharmaceutical Assistance to the Aged and Disabled (PAAD) is the big one. If your income is under $54,943 as a single person or under $62,390 as a married couple, you pay $5 for each covered generic prescription and $7 for each covered brand name drug. If your Part D plan charges less than $5 for a generic, you pay the lower amount.

PAAD works alongside Medicare. If you have Medicare, you must be enrolled in a Part D drug plan. PAAD then pays the monthly premium for certain basic Part D plans priced at or below the regional benchmark. If you are in a Medicare Advantage plan, PAAD contributes up to the benchmark amount toward the drug part of your premium.

PAAD covers prescription drugs, insulin and insulin supplies. It does not pay for diabetic testing supplies such as strips and lancets. Those go through Medicare Part B. You cannot get PAAD if you have Medicaid, or if you have other coverage that is as good or better.

Senior Gold

Senior Gold picks up where PAAD leaves off. It serves people whose income is up to $10,000 above the PAAD limit. You pay $15 plus 50% of the remaining cost of each covered prescription. Once your out-of-pocket costs pass $2,000 in a year ($3,000 for a married couple), you pay a flat $15 per prescription for the rest of your eligibility period. Unlike PAAD, Senior Gold does not pay your Part D premium. You must reapply every year.

Open enrollment matters for PAAD members

Medicare open enrollment runs October 15 to December 7. If you are on PAAD and pick a Part D plan priced above the benchmark, you may owe part of the premium yourself. Free, unbiased counselors at the State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) can compare plans with you. Call 1-800-792-8820.

What is Lifeline utility assistance?

Lifeline pays eligible residents $225 a year toward electric and natural gas costs. The age, disability and income rules match PAAD. If you qualify for PAAD, you very likely qualify for Lifeline too, and the same NJSave application screens you for both. It is a modest amount, but it arrives every year as long as you stay eligible.

One exception: if you receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI), do not apply. Your SSI check already includes a utility supplement of up to $18.75 a month.

If your utility bills are a bigger problem, Lifeline is only the start. Our guide to food and utility help covers heating aid, bill discounts and free weatherization.

Can the state pay my Medicare premium?

Yes, through the Medicare Savings Programs. In 2026, the standard Part B premium is $202.90 a month. That is about $2,435 a year coming out of your Social Security check. These programs can take it off your plate.

ProgramWhat it pays2026 annual income limit (single / couple)
QMB (Qualified Medicare Beneficiary)Part A and Part B premiums, plus deductibles, coinsurance and copays for covered services$15,960 / $21,640
SLMB (Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiary)Part B premium$19,152 / $25,968
QI (Qualifying Individual)Part B premium$21,546 / $29,214

New Jersey's Division of Aging Services lists an asset limit of $9,950 for a single person and $14,910 for a couple. Ask which savings and property count when you apply. You do not need to qualify for full Medicaid to get one of these programs.

There is a bonus. If you are enrolled in any Medicare Savings Program, you automatically qualify for Extra Help with drug costs too.

What is Extra Help?

Extra Help, also called the Part D Low Income Subsidy, is a federal program run through Social Security. It lowers or eliminates your Part D premium and deductible and caps your copays. In 2026, people with full Extra Help pay no more than $5.10 for a generic and $12.65 for a brand name drug. People with full Medicaid and very low income pay $1.60 and $4.90. People getting Medicaid long-term care in a nursing home or through a home care waiver pay nothing.

For 2026, the income limits are about $1,995 a month for one person and $2,705 a month for a couple. The resource limits are $18,090 for one person and $36,100 for a couple. Social Security does not count every dollar of income or every asset, so apply even if you are a little over.

If you get PAAD, apply for Extra Help as well. The two programs work together, and NJSave covers both.

How do I apply with NJSave?

NJSave is New Jersey's single application for older adults and people with disabilities. One form enrolls eligible people in PAAD, Senior Gold, Lifeline, the Medicare Savings Programs, Extra Help and the Hearing Aid Assistance to the Aged and Disabled program. It also screens you for heating aid, the Universal Service Fund and SNAP food benefits.

You can apply online through the NJSave application. A paper version is available if you do not use a computer. Call 1-800-792-9745 and ask for one to be mailed.

  1. Gather proof of income. Bring your Social Security award letter or SSA-1099, pension statements, and recent bank statements showing interest.
  2. Find your Medicare card. You will need your Medicare number and your Part D plan name if you have one.
  3. List your assets. Have bank, savings and investment balances handy for the Medicare Savings Programs and Extra Help.
  4. Apply once. Complete NJSave online or on paper. Answer every question, even if you think a program does not apply to you.
  5. Watch your mail. If approved for PAAD or Senior Gold, you should receive an ID card. Respond quickly to any request for more documents.
Example: a widower in Paterson

Say you are 77, live alone, and your only income is $1,300 a month from Social Security, or $15,600 a year. You have about $6,000 in savings. That puts you under the QMB limit, so the state could pay your Part B premium and your Medicare cost sharing. QMB brings Extra Help with it. The same NJSave application also checks you for PAAD and Lifeline, which could bring copays down to $5 and $7 and add $225 a year.

Example: a couple in Freehold

Say you are both retired, with combined income of $68,000 from Social Security and a pension. That is above the PAAD limit for couples but inside the Senior Gold range. You would keep your own Part D plan and premium, pay $15 plus half the remaining cost of each prescription, and drop to $15 per prescription after spending $3,000 in a year.

What else can NJSave help with?

The same application can pay off in places people do not expect.

Hearing aids

The Hearing Aid Assistance to the Aged and Disabled (HAAAD) program reimburses up to $500 for one hearing aid or $1,000 for two in a calendar year. You must be enrolled in PAAD or Lifeline (if you are not, file an NJSave application first), and you cannot have hearing aid coverage through Medicaid, another insurer or retiree benefits. If you buy another hearing aid in a later year, you file a new application. Call 1-800-792-9745 for the form.

Other perks

The Division of Aging Services says people who qualify for PAAD or Lifeline may also be eligible for reduced motor vehicle fees and low-cost spaying and neutering for pets. Being on PAAD also helps protect you from winter utility shutoffs. Our food and utility guide explains that program. Property tax relief is a separate application, so read our property tax relief guide too.

Quick check: are you leaving money on the table?

If you are 65 or older and your income is under $54,943 (single) or $62,390 (married), you may be eligible for $5 and $7 prescriptions, $225 a year for utilities and up to $1,000 toward hearing aids. If your income is under $21,546 (single) or $29,214 (married) and your savings are modest, the state may also pay your $202.90 Part B premium.

What mistakes should I avoid?

  • Not applying because you think you earn too much. The PAAD limit is far higher than most people expect. Senior Gold goes higher still.
  • Skipping the renewal. Most PAAD members renew every two years. Senior Gold members renew yearly. The form arrives about four months before your card expires. If it has not come at least two months before, call 1-800-792-9745.
  • Picking a Part D plan on price alone. Check that your drugs are on the plan's list. If a drug is not covered, PAAD will not cover it either until your doctor requests an exception or you switch drugs.
  • Forgetting to report changes. A new pension, a move or a death in the family can change your eligibility.
  • Trusting cold callers. No legitimate program will call you out of the blue to sell you a plan or ask for your Medicare number.

For free, one-on-one help, call SHIP at 1-800-792-8820 or the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737. If you suspect Medicare fraud, the New Jersey Senior Medicare Patrol is at 1-732-777-1940, extension 1117.

New to Medicare? Start with our guide to turning 65 in New Jersey and our comparison of Medicare Advantage and Medigap.

faq.q: Do I need a Medicare Part D plan to get PAAD?
faq.a: Yes, if you have Medicare. PAAD pays the premium for certain basic plans at or below the regional benchmark and then limits your copays to $5 generic and $7 brand.

faq.q: Can I get PAAD and a Medicare Savings Program at the same time?
faq.a: Many people qualify for more than one program. NJSave screens you for all of them at once and sorts out how they fit together with your other coverage.

faq.q: What is the difference between QMB, SLMB and QI?
faq.a: QMB has the lowest income limit and pays Part A and B premiums plus most Medicare cost sharing. SLMB and QI pay only the Part B premium but allow higher income.

faq.q: How long does approval take?
faq.a: If you are approved for Senior Gold, you should receive an ID card within about 30 days. Respond quickly to any letter asking for documents to avoid delays.

faq.q: How much can I earn and still get PAAD in 2026?
faq.a: Your income must be under $54,943 if you are single or under $62,390 if you are married. You must be 65 or older, or 18 to 64 and receiving Social Security disability benefits.

faq.q: Does New Jersey help pay for hearing aids?
faq.a: Yes. The HAAAD program reimburses up to $500 for one hearing aid or $1,000 for two in a calendar year for people enrolled in PAAD or Lifeline. Call 1-800-792-9745.

title: Social Security's 3.6% raise for 2027: what it means in NJ
dek: Checks grow in January, but Medicare, the earnings test and your claiming age all shape what you actually keep. Plus how New Jersey taxes retirement income.
keyFacts: 2027 COLA: 3.6%, starting with January 2027 payments
Average retired worker: $2,095 rising to $2,170
2027 Part B premium not yet announced; Trustees projected $209.50
Earnings limit under full retirement age: $25,560
New Jersey does not tax Social Security
body:
Social Security checks will grow by 3.6% in January 2027. The Social Security Administration announced the cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) on October 14, 2026. For the average retired worker, that means about $75 more a month.

Before you plan how to spend it, there are a few things to know. Medicare will take its own increase out of your check. Working while collecting has limits. And New Jersey treats retirement income in its own way. Here is what the new numbers mean for you.

How much bigger will my check be?

Take your current monthly benefit and multiply by 1.036. A $1,500 check becomes about $1,554. A $2,500 check becomes about $2,590. The raise shows up in the payments you receive in January 2027.

Average monthly benefitBefore the COLAFrom January 2027
All retired workers$2,095$2,170
Retired couple, both receiving benefits$3,238$3,355
Widow or widower living alone$1,936$2,005
All disabled workers$1,642$1,701

Supplemental Security Income (SSI) rises too. The federal payment rises to $1,029 a month for an individual and $1,544 for a couple. The maximum benefit for someone retiring at full retirement age in 2027 is $4,188 a month.

Social Security usually sends COLA notices in December. If you have a my Social Security account at ssa.gov/myaccount, you can read yours online. It shows your new gross benefit and what is being taken out for Medicare.

How is the COLA set?

The COLA follows the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers. Social Security compares average prices in July, August and September with the same months a year earlier. The percentage change becomes next year's raise. That is why the number is announced every October.

Your own costs may rise faster or slower than that index. If your rent, property taxes or drug costs jumped this year, the COLA may not cover all of it. That is a good reason to check the state programs in our other benefits guides.

The raise is 3.6%. What lands in your bank account depends on Medicare.

How does Medicare Part B affect my raise?

If you are on Medicare and collecting Social Security, your Part B premium comes straight out of your check. In 2026, the standard premium is $202.90 a month. When it goes up, it eats part of your COLA.

As of mid October, the government has not announced the 2027 Part B premium. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services usually releases it later in the fall. The Medicare Trustees projected a standard premium of $209.50 for 2027. Treat that as an estimate until the official number comes out.

Example: a retired bus driver in Trenton

Say you get $2,000 a month before Medicare. A 3.6% COLA adds $72. If Part B rises to the projected $209.50, your premium goes up $6.60. Your deposit would grow by about $65.40 a month. If the final premium is different, your net raise changes with it.

Two other rules matter here. First, a "hold harmless" provision protects most people from seeing their net check go down because of a Part B increase. Second, people with higher incomes pay an extra amount on top of the standard premium, based on their tax return from two years earlier. If your income dropped because you retired or lost a spouse, you can ask Social Security to use the newer figure.

If paying Medicare premiums is a stretch, New Jersey's Medicare Savings Programs can cover Part B entirely for people with modest incomes. See our guide to prescription and bill help for the 2026 limits. Medicare open enrollment also runs October 15 to December 7, which is the time to review your drug plan or Medicare Advantage plan. Free counseling is available from SHIP at 1-800-792-8820.

Can I work and collect Social Security?

Yes, but if you are younger than full retirement age, Social Security may hold back some benefits. This is called the earnings test. It only counts wages and net self-employment income. Pensions, annuities, investment income and interest do not count.

Your situation in 2027Earnings limitWhat happens above it
Under full retirement age all year$25,560 a year ($2,130 a month)$1 withheld for every $2 over the limit
Reaching full retirement age in 2027$67,920 a year ($5,660 a month)$1 withheld for every $3 over, counting only months before your birthday month
At or past full retirement ageNo limitNothing is withheld

Withheld money is not gone forever. Once you reach full retirement age, Social Security recalculates your benefit to credit you for the months it held back. If you plan to work, tell Social Security your expected earnings so it can adjust your payments and avoid an overpayment later.

When should I claim?

There is no single right age. It depends on your health, your savings, whether you are married and whether you are still working. These are the basic rules.

  • Full retirement age is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later.
  • Claiming at 62 cuts your benefit by 30% for life if your full retirement age is 67. A $1,000 benefit becomes $700.
  • Waiting past full retirement age adds 8% a year until age 70. After 70, there is no benefit to waiting.
  • COLAs apply either way. Each year's raise is a percentage of whatever benefit you lock in, so a bigger starting check gets bigger raises in dollars.
Example: a married couple in Wayne

Say one spouse earned much more over a career. If that higher earner waits until 70, the couple's survivor benefit is larger too. When one spouse dies, the survivor keeps the larger of the two checks. For couples in good health, delaying the higher benefit is often a form of life insurance for the person left behind.

Think about these questions before you file. How long did your parents live, and how is your own health? Do you have savings to cover the years before you claim? Are you still working, and would the earnings test hold back benefits? Does your spouse depend on your record for a survivor check?

Before you decide, log in to your my Social Security account and look at your estimates at 62, 67 and 70. You can also call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 or make an appointment at a local office. A fee-only financial planner can help you see the whole picture.

Does New Jersey tax my Social Security?

No. New Jersey does not tax Social Security benefits at all. The state lists them as exempt income. Federal tax is a separate question, and some retirees owe federal tax on part of their benefits.

New Jersey also lets many retirees exclude pension, annuity and IRA withdrawals from state income tax. You or your spouse must be 62 or older, or disabled under Social Security rules, on the last day of the tax year.

Total NJ incomeMarried filing jointlySingle or head of householdMarried filing separately
$100,000 or lessUp to $100,000Up to $75,000Up to $50,000
$100,001 to $125,00050% of pension37.5% of pension25% of pension
$125,001 to $150,00025% of pension18.75% of pension12.5% of pension
Over $150,000Not eligibleNot eligibleNot eligible

If you do not use your full pension exclusion, you may be able to use the rest against other income through the Other Retirement Income Exclusion. To qualify, you must be 62 or older, have total income of $150,000 or less, and have $3,000 or less from wages and business income. The NJ-1040 instructions include a worksheet.

Example: a single retiree in Cherry Hill

Say you are 66 and receive $30,000 a year in Social Security plus a $40,000 pension. New Jersey ignores the Social Security, so your total state income is $40,000. That is under $100,000, so you can exclude up to $75,000 of pension income. Your whole $40,000 pension is excluded, and you would owe no New Jersey income tax on it.

What else changes in 2027?

The COLA is the headline, but Social Security adjusts several other numbers each January. These matter most if you are still working or helping a parent who gets SSI.

Item20262027
Maximum earnings taxed for Social Security$184,500$192,300
Earnings needed for one work credit$1,890$1,970
Maximum benefit at full retirement age$4,152 a month$4,188 a month
SSI federal payment, individual / couple$994 / $1,491$1,029 / $1,544
SSI resource limit, individual / couple$2,000 / $3,000$2,000 / $3,000 (unchanged)

Work credits matter if you are close to the 40 credits needed for retirement benefits, or for premium-free Medicare Part A. You can earn up to four credits a year. In 2027 that takes $7,880 in earnings.

On the Medicare side, the Trustees also projected the 2027 Part B deductible at $292, up from $283. Like the premium, that is an estimate until the government announces the final figure.

What should I do now?

  1. Open or check your my Social Security account. Watch for your COLA notice in December.
  2. Review your Medicare coverage by December 7. Plan costs and drug lists change every year.
  3. Check New Jersey help you may be missing. The PAS-1 deadline for property tax relief was November 2, 2026. If you missed it, call 1-888-238-1233 and watch for the next application. Our property tax relief guide walks you through it.
  4. Update your budget. Use your net deposit, after Medicare, as your real raise.
  5. Ignore anyone who calls about your COLA. Social Security will not call, text or email to ask for your number or a payment. Read our guide to scams in New Jersey.

faq.q: When will I see the 3.6% increase?
faq.a: In the payments you receive in January 2027. Social Security usually sends notices in December, and you can see yours in your my Social Security account.

faq.q: Has the 2027 Medicare Part B premium been announced?
faq.a: Not as of mid October 2026. It is expected later in the fall. The Medicare Trustees projected $209.50 a month, up from $202.90 in 2026.

faq.q: Does New Jersey tax Social Security?
faq.a: No. Social Security is exempt from New Jersey income tax. Many retirees 62 and older can also exclude pension and IRA income if total income is $150,000 or less.

faq.q: If I earn too much and benefits are withheld, do I lose that money?
faq.a: No. When you reach full retirement age, Social Security recalculates your benefit to credit the months it withheld.

faq.q: What is the 2027 earnings limit if I work and collect Social Security?
faq.a: If you are under full retirement age all year, the limit is $25,560. In the year you reach full retirement age it is $67,920, counting only earnings before that month. There is no limit once you reach full retirement age.

faq.q: How much will the average check go up in 2027?
faq.a: The average retired worker's benefit rises from about $2,095 to $2,170 a month, an increase of about $75. Your Medicare Part B premium may take part of that.

title: Food and utility help for New Jersey seniors: where to start
dek: SNAP, senior meals, farmers market benefits, heating aid and free weatherization can all ease a tight budget. Here is how each works and how to apply this season.
keyFacts: NJ SNAP minimum benefit: $95 a month
Households with someone 60+ skip SNAP's gross income test
LIHEAP/USF season: October 1, 2026, to June 30, 2027
Energy aid income limit for one person: $51,273
Energy help line: 1-800-510-3102
body:
Groceries and heating bills hit fixed incomes hard. New Jersey has a long list of programs that help, and many older adults qualify for more than one. The trick is knowing where to start. Most of these programs share applications, and one phone call can open several doors.

This guide covers food benefits, meals, heating and electric help, free home energy upgrades and water bills. It also shows you what to bring when you apply.

Can I get SNAP as an older adult?

Yes, and the rules are friendlier for people 60 and older. SNAP (the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, once called food stamps) puts money on an EBT card for groceries. In New Jersey, eligible households get at least $95 a month. The federal maximum for a one-person household from October 2026 is $306 a month.

Special rules for households with someone 60 or older

  • No gross income test. A household with a member 60 or older, or with a disability, can qualify even if its income is above the standard limits. Only the net income test applies, after deductions.
  • Medical costs count. Out-of-pocket medical expenses above $35 a month can be deducted. That can include costs such as Medicare premiums, copays and prescriptions.
  • Housing costs count in full. Rent, mortgage, property taxes and utilities can all lower your countable income, with no cap for older households.
  • Longer approvals. Older adults' cases can last 24 months before renewal.
  • You can apply on your own. An older adult living with family may be able to apply as a separate household in some situations.
A note on work rules

A 2025 federal law expanded SNAP work requirements to adults up to age 64 without young dependents. Covered adults must log 80 hours a month of work, training or volunteering unless they qualify for an exemption, such as a disability or medical condition. People 65 and older are exempt. If you are 60 to 64, ask your county agency how the rule applies to you.

Apply through your County Board of Social Services. You can usually complete the process by phone or online, without an in-person visit. Free SNAP Navigators can help you fill out the form. Find local help through the state's SNAP help page.

Many older adults skip SNAP because they assume they will only get a few dollars. In New Jersey, the minimum is $95 a month, or $1,140 a year. Medical and housing deductions often push the amount higher.

What about farmers market vouchers?

The Senior Farmers Market Nutrition Program gives low-income adults 60 and older money to spend on fresh, locally grown fruits, vegetables and herbs at approved farmers markets and farm stands. Household income must be under 185% of the federal poverty level. In 2026, Bergen and Gloucester counties gave $40 per person, now loaded as an e-benefit or QR code instead of paper vouchers.

The program runs through your county office on aging, usually in early summer, and benefits go first come, first served. This year's season has mostly wrapped up, so call your county in late spring to get on the list for 2027.

Where can I get meals?

Congregate meals

Senior centers, churches and community sites across the state serve hot meals to adults 60 and older and their spouses of any age. There is no fixed price. You contribute what you can afford. Meals are served at least once a day, five or more days a week, and many sites ask you to reserve a day ahead. They are a good way to see friends, too.

Home-delivered meals

If illness, disability or isolation keeps you at home, you may qualify for home-delivered meals, often called Meals on Wheels. Adults 60 and older are eligible after a needs assessment. Programs deliver at least one meal a day, five days a week, and some add weekend meals. The meals are federally funded, with a suggested contribution.

Both meal programs run through your county Area Agency on Aging. Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 to reach yours.

Food banks and senior food boxes

Food banks supply the local pantries in your town. Some also run the Commodity Supplemental Food Program, which provides monthly food boxes for older adults through local sites. It is not offered everywhere, so call to ask about a site near you.

Food bankCountiesPhone

Community FoodBank of New Jersey, Southern Branch (Egg Harbor)Atlantic, Cape May, Cumberland609-383-8843
Fulfill (Neptune)Monmouth, Ocean732-918-2600

If your county is not listed, dial 2-1-1 for the nearest pantry.

How do I get help with heating and electric bills?

New Jersey bundles three programs into one application. The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) helps with heating costs. The Universal Service Fund (USF) lowers your monthly gas and electric bills. The Weatherization Assistance Program makes free energy-saving repairs. Check the weatherization box on the form to be considered for all three.

Applications for this season are open from October 1, 2026, to June 30, 2027, and help is first come, first served. Apply early.

Household sizeAnnual income limitMonthly income limit
1 person$51,273$4,273
2 people$67,049$5,587
3 people$82,825$6,902
  • LIHEAP heating help depends on your income, household size, fuel type and region. It can be paid to your utility or, for oil and propane, by check to you and your supplier.
  • Medically necessary cooling pays a fixed $300 if someone in the home needs air conditioning for health reasons.
  • USF credits help pay gas and electric costs above a set share of your income, up to $200 a month.

Apply online at energyassistance.nj.gov, or call 1-800-510-3102 to find your local agency. Applicants 60 and older, or with a disability, may apply by mail or ask for a home visit.

Other energy programs to know

  • Comfort Partners offers a free home energy visit and upgrades to help lower bills. Income must be at or below 250% of the federal poverty level, about $39,900 a year for one person in 2026. You need an individually metered gas or electric account. Call 1-866-378-4345. If you heat with oil, propane or kerosene, use the state weatherization program instead.
  • NJ SHARES helps households that earn too much for LIHEAP and USF, roughly 200% to 400% of the poverty level, who have fallen behind. Call 1-866-657-4273.
  • PAGE (Payment Assistance for Gas and Electric) helps low and moderate income residents who are at least 45 days behind or have a shutoff notice. Dial 2-1-1 for the current intake agency.
  • Lifeline pays $225 a year toward utilities if you are 65 or older, or on Social Security disability, with income under $54,943 single or $62,390 married. It is part of the NJSave application described in our guide to prescription and bill help.

Protection from winter shutoffs

New Jersey's Winter Termination Program protects eligible customers from gas and electric shutoffs from November 15 to March 15. You are covered if you receive LIHEAP, USF, PAAD, Lifeline, SSI or several other benefits. Households that cannot pay because of illness, medical bills, job loss or a death in the family may also qualify. Call your utility to make sure you are enrolled, or reach the Board of Public Utilities at 1-800-624-0241.

The protection pauses shutoffs. It does not erase the bill. Pay what you can each month so you do not face a large balance on March 16.

If the bill is already overdue, call before the shutoff notice, not after.

Is there help with water bills?

New Jersey's Department of Community Affairs ran a Low Income Household Water Assistance Program (LIHWAP) with temporary federal funds. The state's current energy assistance page does not list it. Call 1-800-510-3102 to ask whether any water help is open now.

Also call your water utility or town water department directly. Many offer payment plans, and some towns run their own assistance. Keep paying what you can each month while you wait for an answer.

How do I apply, and what should I bring?

  1. Collect proof of income. Your Social Security award letter or SSA-1099, pension statements and any wage stubs for everyone in the household.
  2. Gather your bills. Recent gas, electric and water bills, plus your fuel oil delivery receipts if you have them.
  3. Show your housing costs. Lease, mortgage statement or property tax bill.
  4. Save medical receipts. For SNAP, list Medicare premiums, copays, pharmacy costs and medical transportation.
  5. Bring ID. A photo ID and Social Security numbers for household members who are applying.
  6. Apply to everything you may qualify for. Start with the energy application and SNAP. Then call your county office on aging about meals and next year's farmers market benefits.
Example: a widow in Vineland

Say you are 74, live alone, and get $1,900 a month from Social Security. You heat with oil and have steady pharmacy bills. At $22,800 a year, you are well under the $51,273 LIHEAP limit, so you could get heating help and free weatherization. Because you are over 60, SNAP skips the gross income test and counts your medical and housing costs, so you may also qualify for at least $95 a month in food benefits. Your county office on aging can tell you about meal sites near you.

If you get stuck, dial 2-1-1 (or 1-877-652-1148) any time, or call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737. For more ways to stretch a budget, see our guides to property tax relief and free and discounted things to do in New Jersey.

faq.q: Do I have to visit an office to apply for SNAP?
faq.a: Usually not. New Jersey lets you complete the SNAP process by phone or online. A free SNAP Navigator can help you with the form.

faq.q: Does LIHEAP help with oil or propane heat?
faq.a: Yes. LIHEAP covers oil, propane and other fuels. Payments for delivered fuel are typically made by check to you and your supplier together.

faq.q: Who can get home-delivered meals?
faq.a: Adults 60 and older who are homebound because of illness, disability or isolation, after a needs assessment. Call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county program.

faq.q: Is there a deadline for energy assistance?
faq.a: The 2026 to 2027 application period runs from October 1, 2026, to June 30, 2027, but help is first come, first served, so apply early.

faq.q: Can the utility shut off my heat in winter?
faq.a: If you are enrolled in the Winter Termination Program, your gas and electric service is protected from shutoff from November 15 to March 15. People on LIHEAP, USF, PAAD, Lifeline or SSI qualify. Call your utility or the Board of Public Utilities at 1-800-624-0241.

faq.q: What is the minimum SNAP benefit in New Jersey?
faq.a: New Jersey sets a minimum of $95 a month, or $1,140 a year, for eligible households. Medical and housing deductions often push older adults above the minimum.

title: Benefits for older veterans in New Jersey
dek: Tax breaks, VA pension with Aid and Attendance, veterans homes and burial benefits for older New Jersey veterans and surviving spouses.
keyFacts: Honorably discharged veterans who own a NJ home can get $250 a year off property taxes.
100% disabled veterans may owe no property tax on their main home.
NJ gives honorably discharged veterans a $6,000 state income tax exemption.
VA pension with Aid and Attendance pays up to $29,093 a year for a single veteran (2025 to 2026 rate).
body:
If you served in the military, or were married to someone who did, New Jersey and the federal government both offer benefits that can make retirement easier. Some are small but steady, like a yearly property tax deduction. Others, like a VA pension with Aid and Attendance, can help pay for care. Here are the main ones, and where to get free help.

A note on names: state veterans programs used to sit inside the Department of Military and Veterans Affairs (DMAVA). The New Jersey Department of Veterans Affairs (NJDVA) became its own department on January 9, 2026, so you may see both names.

Can I get the $250 veterans property tax deduction?

New Jersey takes up to $250 a year off the property tax bill of qualifying veterans. You may be eligible if, as of October 1 of the year before the tax year, you:

  • Had active duty service in the U.S. Armed Forces and were honorably discharged.
  • Own the home, in whole or in part.
  • Are a legal resident of New Jersey.

You no longer need to have served during a war. Voters approved that change in November 2020, and it took effect December 4, 2020. Reserve or Guard training alone generally does not count unless you were called to federal active duty.

A surviving spouse, civil union partner or domestic partner can keep claiming it if they have not remarried or formed a new civil union or domestic partnership. The veteran must have been a New Jersey resident at death.

How to apply: fill out Form V.S.S. and give it to your town's tax assessor between October 1 and December 31 of the year before, or to the tax collector during the tax year itself. Bring your DD-214, your deed and proof of residency, such as a driver's license. Survivors also bring the death certificate and marriage certificate.

Also see our guides to property tax relief, ANCHOR, the Senior Freeze and Stay NJ.

What if I am a 100% disabled veteran?

A veteran who is 100% permanently and totally disabled from a service-connected disability may pay no property tax on their main home. The rules say you:

  • Had active duty service and were honorably discharged.
  • Have the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) certify your service-connected disability.
  • Own the home, in whole or in part, and live there as your principal residence.
  • Are a legal resident of New Jersey.

The un-remarried surviving spouse, civil union partner or domestic partner of a veteran who met these rules may also qualify, as long as the veteran owned and lived in a New Jersey home at death. File Form D.V.S.S.E. with your municipal tax assessor at any time during the year. In a two or more family house, it covers only the share you live in.

Is there a veterans income tax break in New Jersey?

Yes. The New Jersey Division of Taxation gives honorably discharged veterans a $6,000 exemption on the state income tax return, on top of other exemptions.

To claim it, fill in the veteran oval on your return and send proof of honorable discharge, usually your DD-214, the first time. Upload it online using notice code VET, mail it to NJ Division of Taxation, Veteran Exemption, PO Box 440, Trenton, NJ 08646-0440, or fax it to 609-633-8427.

A surviving spouse can claim it only for the year the veteran died, on a joint return.

What is VA pension with Aid and Attendance?

The VA pension is a monthly payment for wartime veterans with limited income and savings. Aid and Attendance and Housebound are extra amounts for people who need more help. Un-remarried surviving spouses can get a survivors pension with the same add-ons.

To get the basic veterans pension, you generally need:

  • A discharge that was not dishonorable.
  • At least 90 days of active duty, with at least one day in a wartime period, if you started before September 8, 1980. Later service has a 24 month rule with exceptions.
  • To be 65 or older, permanently and totally disabled, in a nursing home for long-term care, or getting SSDI or SSI.
  • Income and net worth under limits set by Congress. The net worth limit is $163,699 through November 30, 2026, not counting your home or car.

Wartime periods include World War II, Korea (June 27, 1950, to January 31, 1955), the Vietnam era (August 5, 1964, to May 7, 1975, or from November 1, 1955, for service in Vietnam) and the Gulf War (August 2, 1990, onward).

Aid and Attendance may apply if you need another person's help with things like bathing, eating or dressing, if illness keeps you in bed much of the day, if you live in a nursing home because of a disability, or if your eyesight is severely limited. Housebound is for people who spend most of their time at home because of a permanent disability. You cannot get both at once.

How much it pays. The VA sets a yearly ceiling called the Maximum Annual Pension Rate (MAPR). Your pension is the MAPR minus your countable yearly income, divided into 12 monthly payments. These are the VA's rates effective December 1, 2025:

WhoBasic pensionHouseboundAid and Attendance
Veteran, no dependents$17,441 a year$21,313 a year$29,093 a year
Veteran with one dependent (such as a spouse)$22,839 a year$26,710 a year$34,488 a year
Surviving spouse, no dependents$11,699 a year$14,298 a year$18,697 a year

How to apply: apply online at va.gov, in person at a VA regional office, or by mail to the Pension Intake Center, PO Box 5365, Janesville, WI 53547-5365. For Aid and Attendance or Housebound, a medical examiner fills out part of VA Form 21-2680. Nursing home residents also send VA Form 21-0779. Survivors use VA Form 21P-534EZ.

How do I sign up for VA health care?

You may qualify for VA health care if you served in the active military and did not receive a dishonorable discharge. Those who enlisted after September 7, 1980, generally need 24 continuous months of service, with exceptions. Having other insurance does not affect your VA benefits.

Apply online, call 877-222-8387 (Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Eastern), mail VA Form 10-10EZ, or bring it to a VA medical center or clinic.

What do NJ veterans homes and service offices offer?

Veterans Memorial Homes. New Jersey runs three long-term care homes for honorably discharged veterans of war or peacetime service, their spouses and widows or widowers, and Gold Star parents. Spouses must be at least 50 and have been married to the veteran for at least 10 years. Cost is based on ability to pay, and people who lived in New Jersey for two years before applying get preference.

  • Menlo Park, 132 Evergreen Road, Edison. Admissions 732-452-4272.
  • Paramus, 1 Veterans Drive, Paramus. Admissions 201-634-8435.
  • Vineland, 524 North West Boulevard, Vineland. Admissions 856-405-4217.

None of the three homes takes NJ Medicaid or Medicare Advantage plans, according to their admissions pages. Each home suggests having Medicare Parts A and B with secondary insurance and drug coverage, so ask the home about payment before you apply. Our guides to housing options and care costs can help you compare.

Veterans Service Offices. The state has a Veterans Service Office in each of New Jersey's 21 counties. Staff help veterans and families find local, state and federal benefits. Call toll free 844-671-1019 or the NJ Veterans Benefits Hotline at 888-865-8387 (888-8NJ-VETS).

Transportation. Most counties offer veterans free rides to VA medical centers, clinics, pharmacies and doctors. Ask your county Veterans Service Officer how to book.

Where can a veteran be buried in New Jersey?

The Brigadier General William C. Doyle Veterans Memorial Cemetery is at 350 Provinceline Road, Wrightstown, in Burlington County. Eligible veterans whose service ended under conditions other than dishonorable can be buried there, along with their spouse and certain dependent children. The person being buried, veteran or family member, must have been a New Jersey legal resident at death or have lived at least half of their life in the state. Our veterans burial benefits guide has the full rules.

Burial is free unless the family chooses not to use the state-provided grave liner. Graves cannot be reserved, but pre-registering at the cemetery or a Veterans Service Office is encouraged. When the time comes, the funeral director calls the Interment Office at 609-738-2400.

How do I get help for free and avoid pension scams?

The VA says accredited Veterans Service Organization representatives always help with VA claims for free. Accredited attorneys and claims agents may charge fees. Find one with the VA's online search tool.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) warns about people who go after veterans' pensions. Some lawyers, financial planners and insurance agents hold free seminars at senior centers or assisted living communities and urge veterans over 65 to move money into trusts or insurance products to qualify for Aid and Attendance. That can cost you Medicaid eligibility, tie up your savings for a long time and carry fees of hundreds to thousands of dollars. The FTC's advice: treat pressure to act fast as your cue to say no. For more warning signs, see our scams guide.

faq.q: Do I need wartime service for the New Jersey $250 veterans property tax deduction?
faq.a: No. Since December 4, 2020, honorably discharged veterans with active duty service qualify without serving during a war. You must own the home and be a New Jersey resident as of October 1 of the year before.

faq.q: Can a widow of a veteran get the veterans property tax deduction in New Jersey?
faq.a: Yes, if she has not remarried or entered a new civil union or domestic partnership, owns the home, lives in New Jersey, and the veteran was a New Jersey resident at death. File Form V.S.S. with the town tax assessor.

faq.q: Who qualifies for VA Aid and Attendance?
faq.a: You must get a VA pension and need help with daily activities like bathing or dressing, be largely bedbound, live in a nursing home due to disability, or have severely limited eyesight. Surviving spouses on a survivors pension can qualify too.

faq.q: Should I pay someone to help me apply for VA benefits?
faq.a: You do not need to. The VA says accredited Veterans Service Organization representatives help with claims for free, and New Jersey has a Veterans Service Office in every county. Be wary of anyone urging you to move assets to qualify.

title: How to find an elder law attorney in New Jersey
dek: What elder law attorneys do, when your family needs one, county bar referral numbers, free legal help for older adults, and the questions to ask before you hire.
keyFacts: Every New Jersey county is covered by a bar association lawyer referral line. Call the one where your parent lives.
New Jersey's Supreme Court does not certify lawyers in elder law. Look for the Certified Elder Law Attorney (CELA) credential from the National Elder Law Foundation.
Legal Services of New Jersey offers free civil legal help to low income residents at 1-888-576-5529.
County Area Agencies on Aging must offer legal help for low income adults over 60. Call 1-877-222-3737.
NJ FamilyCare looks back five years at asset transfers when someone applies for long term care.
body:
An elder law attorney is a lawyer who focuses on the legal problems that come with getting older. That usually means paying for long term care, Medicaid (NJ FamilyCare) planning, powers of attorney and health care directives, guardianship, special needs trusts and protecting an older adult from exploitation.

In New Jersey, you can find one through your county bar association's lawyer referral service, the National Academy of Elder Law Attorneys directory, or the National Elder Law Foundation's list of certified elder law attorneys. If money is tight, Legal Services of New Jersey offers free help to people with low incomes at 1-888-576-5529.

General information, not legal advice

A New Jersey attorney who knows your family's situation can tell you what fits.

What does an elder law attorney do?

An elder law attorney looks at the whole picture of an older adult's health, money and family, then plans for what is likely to come next. A general practice lawyer may write a will. An elder law attorney also asks how your mom would pay for a nursing home.

Common work includes:

  • Planning documents. Wills, durable powers of attorney, advance directives and trusts. Our estate planning guide covers the basics.
  • Medicaid and long term care planning. Helping a person qualify for NJ FamilyCare's Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) program for home care, assisted living or nursing home care, while protecting a spouse at home.
  • Guardianship. Filing for guardianship, representing an older adult in a guardianship case, or finding an alternative. See our guardianship guide.
  • Special needs trusts. Setting aside money for a person with a disability, such as an adult child, without cutting off their public benefits.
  • Benefits and appeals. Medicaid denials, Medicare coverage disputes and other benefit problems.
  • Protection. Stopping financial exploitation, undoing a bad transfer, or dealing with a family member who is misusing a power of attorney.
  • Housing and residents' rights. Nursing home admission contracts, discharges and assisted living agreements.

When does a family need an elder law attorney?

The best time is before a crisis, while your parent can still sign documents. The most common time is right after one, such as a fall, a hospital stay or a dementia diagnosis.

Call one if any of these sound familiar:

  • Your parent has no power of attorney or advance directive, or the ones they have are decades old.
  • Your parent may need a nursing home or full time home care in the next few years, and you do not know how it will be paid for.
  • One parent needs care and the other is healthy and worried about being left with nothing.
  • Someone has given away money or property recently, or is thinking about it. NJ FamilyCare looks back five years at transfers when someone applies for long term care, and gifts in that window can delay coverage.
  • Memory loss is getting worse and nobody has legal authority to act. Guardianship may be the next step.
  • A family member, caregiver or new "friend" seems to have too much control over your parent's money.
  • Your parent wants to leave money to a child or grandchild with a disability.
The cheapest elder law visit is usually the one you make before anything goes wrong.

Say your mom is 82 and has just been diagnosed with early Alzheimer's. She can still understand and sign papers. A meeting now can put a power of attorney and health care directive in place, map out how care might be paid for, and possibly spare the family a guardianship case later. Our guide on dementia support in New Jersey covers the other early steps.

How do I find an elder law attorney in New Jersey?

Start with your county bar association's lawyer referral service, then check national elder law directories. Ask friends, your parent's doctor or a geriatric care manager for names, and compare at least two.

County bar lawyer referral services

The New Jersey State Bar Association does not recommend individual lawyers. It points the public to county referral services instead and asks you to call the one in your own county. These are the numbers it lists as of October 2026:

National directories

  • National Academy of Elder Law Attorneys (NAELA). A membership group for lawyers in elder and special needs law. Its member directory lets you search by ZIP code. Membership shows interest in the field. It is not a certification.
  • National Elder Law Foundation (NELF). Grants the Certified Elder Law Attorney (CELA) credential. NELF says it is the only national organization accredited by the American Bar Association to certify lawyers in elder and special needs law. Its website has a search for certified attorneys.

New Jersey's own Supreme Court certifies lawyers in only a short list of fields, mostly trial work. Elder law is not one of them, so a CELA is the main credential to look for. According to the American Bar Association, earning it takes years of elder law practice, a demanding exam and references from other lawyers.

Can we get free legal help for an older parent?

Yes, if your parent's income is low. Legal Services of New Jersey and county programs for adults over 60 give free help with many civil legal problems.

  • Legal Services of New Jersey hotline. Call 1-888-576-5529 (1-888-LSNJ-LAW) or apply online at lsnjlawhotline.org. It offers free civil legal help to low income New Jersey residents.
  • Your county Area Agency on Aging. Each one must run a legal assistance program for low income adults over 60. Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 to reach yours.
  • LSNJLAW. The free lsnjlaw.org site explains many senior legal topics in plain language.

Free programs are often busy and may not take every kind of case, such as complex Medicaid planning for someone with significant savings. If they cannot help, ask who they would call.

What should I ask an elder law attorney before hiring one?

Ask how much of their practice is elder law, who will actually do the work, and exactly how they charge. Get the fee arrangement in writing before work starts.

  • How many years have you practiced elder law, and about what share of your work is it?
  • Are you a Certified Elder Law Attorney, or a NAELA member?
  • Have you handled cases like ours, such as a Medicaid application with a spouse at home, or a contested guardianship?
  • Who is your client? If an adult child brings a parent in, the lawyer usually represents the parent, and should meet with the parent alone at some point.
  • Will you, a newer associate or a paralegal handle our file? Who returns calls?
  • Do you charge a flat fee or by the hour? What is included, and what costs extra?
  • Is the first meeting free or paid, and how long is it?
  • What do you need from us before the first meeting?

How do elder law fees work?

Fees vary a great deal by firm, county and type of work. Many lawyers charge a flat fee for a package of documents and bill by the hour for open ended work such as litigation or guardianship. Ask for an estimate in writing. Under New Jersey's professional conduct rules, a lawyer who has not regularly represented you must give you the basis of the fee in writing within a reasonable time.

If you later think a bill is too high, New Jersey has a fee arbitration program under the state Supreme Court. Legal Services of New Jersey describes it as cheaper and faster than going to court.

How do I check a lawyer and avoid planning scams?

Look up the lawyer's public discipline history and be wary of anyone who pushes a product. Legal advice should come from a licensed New Jersey lawyer.

  • Check discipline. The Disciplinary Review Board's public lookup shows New Jersey lawyers who have faced public discipline or reinstatement since 1988.
  • Be careful with free seminars. A "free lunch" talk on protecting your savings from nursing homes may really be a pitch for annuities or other financial products. Ask whether the speaker is a lawyer and what they sell.
  • Watch for pressure. Be wary of anyone who rushes your parent to sign, moves money quickly, or wants to be named on accounts. Our guide to scams aimed at older adults in New Jersey lists more warning signs.
  • Complaints. To report a lawyer's conduct, call the Judiciary's attorney ethics and fee arbitration hotline at 1-800-406-8594.

Not sure if you need a lawyer yet? A geriatric care manager can assess your parent's needs first, and you can browse other professionals on our Find care help page. For the cost side of care, see what senior care costs in New Jersey.
