title: Retirement planning in New Jersey: a practical checklist
dek: Social Security at 62 to 70, Medicare at 65, required withdrawals at 73, and New Jersey's property taxes in between. Here is the order of decisions and where to get free, unbiased help.
keyFacts: Social Security can start at 62; full retirement age is 67 if born 1960 or later
Waiting past full retirement age adds 8% a year until 70
Medicare sign-up window: 7 months around your 65th birthday
Required minimum distributions start at 73
Free Medicare counseling (NJ SHIP): 1-800-792-8820
body:
A good retirement plan in New Jersey comes down to a handful of dates and a few local costs. Social Security can start at 62, Medicare sign-up opens three months before 65, and withdrawals from most retirement accounts must begin at 73. Property taxes are the big New Jersey expense, and the state has several programs that soften them.

This checklist is for older adults and the grown children helping them. It walks through each decision in the order it usually comes up, with the official rules and free places to get advice. It is general information, not financial or legal advice. For choices about investments or when to claim, talk with a qualified professional you have checked out.

What should be on a retirement checklist, year by year?

Most of the big deadlines fall between 62 and 73. Put them on a calendar now, with a reminder a few months ahead of each one.

  1. Age 60 to 61. Open a my Social Security account at ssa.gov to see benefit estimates. Gather pension statements and records of what you contributed to pensions and IRAs. You will need them at tax time.
  2. Age 62. Earliest age to start Social Security, at a reduced amount. New Jersey's pension exclusion also opens at 62.
  3. Three months before 65. Your seven-month Medicare sign-up window begins.
  4. Age 65. Medicare starts. An extra $1,000 New Jersey income tax exemption applies. Most state property tax programs for older homeowners also use 65 as the age line.
  5. Age 66 to 67. Full retirement age for Social Security, depending on birth year. It is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later.
  6. Age 70. Delayed retirement credits stop. Waiting past 70 does not raise the benefit.
  7. Age 73. Required minimum distributions from traditional IRAs and most workplace plans begin.

When should my parent claim Social Security?

Any time from 62 to 70. Claiming at 62 cuts the monthly benefit for life, by 30% for people born in 1960 or later. Waiting past full retirement age adds 8% a year until 70.

Here is how the Social Security Administration shows it for someone born in 1960 or later, using a $1,000 benefit at full retirement age.

Start atMonthly benefit
62$700
67 (full retirement age)$1,000
70About $1,240

The figure at 70 adds three years of delayed credits at 8% each. Cost-of-living raises come on top of all of these. There is no single right age. Health, savings, a spouse's benefit and whether your parent is still working all matter. The SSA's online calculator and my Social Security account show personal estimates.

  • Apply ahead. You can apply up to four months before you want benefits to start, online or by calling 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778).
  • Working while collecting. Before full retirement age, earnings above a yearly limit reduce benefits for a time. Our guide to Social Security in 2027 has the new limits, and working after 60 covers jobs and rights.
  • State tax. New Jersey does not tax Social Security at all.

How do we avoid Medicare late penalties?

Sign up during the seven-month window around 65, unless your parent has job-based coverage from current work. Missing it can mean a Part B penalty of 10% for each full year without coverage, usually for life.

The window starts three months before the month your parent turns 65 and ends three months after it. If your parent starts Social Security at least four months before 65, Parts A and B usually start automatically and the card comes in the mail. If not, they must sign up through Social Security.

  • Part B penalty: an extra 10% of the standard premium for each full 12 months they could have had Part B but did not. In 2026 that premium is $202.90 a month.
  • Part D penalty: 1% of a national base amount for each month without drug coverage that is as good as Medicare's, after a gap of 63 days or more.
  • Still working at 65: people covered by a current employer plan (their own or a spouse's) get a special window of eight months after the job or coverage ends. COBRA and retiree coverage do not count as current employer coverage.

Our Medicare 101 guide has a month-by-month timeline. The next choice, between a Medicare Advantage plan and a Medigap policy, is covered in Medicare Advantage or Medigap?.

Delaying Social Security is a choice. Delaying Medicare without job coverage usually costs money for life.

When do required minimum distributions start?

Under current federal law, at 73. The first withdrawal can wait until April 1 of the next year, but the second is still due December 31 of that same year.

The rules, from the IRS:

  • Which accounts: traditional, SEP and SIMPLE IRAs, plus 401(k), 403(b) and 457(b) plans. Roth IRAs have no required withdrawals while the owner is alive.
  • Still working: someone still employed can usually delay withdrawals from that employer's plan until they retire, unless they own 5% or more of the business. This does not apply to IRAs.
  • How much: the prior December 31 balance divided by a life expectancy factor from IRS Publication 590-B. The custodian may calculate it, but the account owner is responsible for getting it right.
  • Missed withdrawal: an excise tax of 25% of the amount not taken, cut to 10% if corrected within two years. The IRS can waive it for a reasonable error that is being fixed, using Form 5329.
Watch the timing

Say your dad turns 73 in 2027 and waits until March 2028 for his first withdrawal. He must take the second one by December 31, 2028. Two withdrawals in one year raise his income, and in New Jersey that can push total income over the $150,000 limit for the pension exclusion. Our guide to how New Jersey taxes retirement income explains that limit.

What does retirement cost in New Jersey?

Property taxes are usually the largest New Jersey line item. Several state programs help homeowners 65 and older, and the state income tax goes easy on most retirement income.

When you build a budget with your mom or dad, list these separately:

  • Property taxes, and the relief against them. ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ are filed together on one form. See our property tax relief guide and the $250 senior deduction.
  • Medicare costs. The Part B premium, deductibles and either a Medigap or Advantage premium. Lower income households should check Medicare Savings Programs and PAAD and Senior Gold.
  • State income tax. Often small or zero for people 62 and older under $100,000 in total income, because of the retirement exclusion.
  • Home repairs and help at home. Our aging in place guide covers modifications.

Staying or moving: the tax facts

Families often weigh a move out of state. These are facts, not advice either way:

  • New Jersey does not tax a nonresident's pension, annuity or IRA income, even if it was earned from work in New Jersey.
  • New Jersey's estate tax ended for deaths on or after January 1, 2018. The state inheritance tax still applies, and how much depends on who inherits and how they are related.
  • Senior Freeze and Stay NJ are only for people who own and live in a New Jersey home. Leaving means giving them up. Senior Freeze also requires owning and living in the same home for several years before you first qualify, so a new home in New Jersey restarts that clock.

If a move is on the table, our guide to selling the family home covers the steps.

How do I check a financial adviser in New Jersey?

Look the person and the firm up before handing over any money. Three free official databases show licenses, job history and any discipline.

  1. FINRA BrokerCheck. Shows whether a person or firm is registered to sell securities or give investment advice, plus complaints and regulatory actions. Help line 1-800-289-9999.
  2. SEC Investment Adviser Public Disclosure. Search adviser firms and representatives and read the firm's Form ADV, which lists fees and disciplinary history.
  3. New Jersey Bureau of Securities. The state regulator for investment professionals in New Jersey. Call toll free in New Jersey at 1-866-446-8378 (1-866-I-INVEST), or 973-504-3600 from outside the state, to check a professional or file a complaint.

BrokerCheck lists only certain criminal and financial matters, so a plain internet search is worth doing too.

Red flags with retirement money

  • A "guaranteed" high return with no risk.
  • Pressure to move money out of a pension, IRA or annuity quickly.
  • A new online friend or romantic partner who brings up an investment. The Bureau of Securities warns about romance scams that turn into investment pitches.
  • Anyone who asks for payment in gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency.

Our guide to common scams explains how to report fraud. And before you assume an old account is gone, search for it. Forgotten bank accounts and insurance payouts often sit with the state, as our guide to unclaimed property in New Jersey explains.

Where can we get free, unbiased retirement help in New Jersey?

Several free services sell nothing. Start with these before paying for advice.

Help withCall
Medicare choices (NJ SHIP)1-800-792-8820
Social Security1-800-772-1213
Medicare1-800-633-4227
Free tax preparation (AARP Tax-Aide)1-888-227-7669
NJ income tax questions609-292-6400
Checking an adviser (NJ)1-866-446-8378

NJ SHIP counselors help people with Medicare compare plans and costs at no charge. AARP Foundation Tax-Aide prepares federal and New Jersey returns for free during tax season, and you do not need to be an AARP member. See our guide to free tax help for sites and what to bring.

If your parent's plan also needs a will, power of attorney or health care directive, our estate planning basics guide explains each document.

faq.q: What is full retirement age for Social Security?
faq.a: It is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later. For people born from 1955 to 1959 it falls between 66 and 2 months and 66 and 10 months. You can start as early as 62 with a smaller benefit, or wait until 70 for a larger one.

faq.q: How do I help my mom avoid a Medicare penalty?
faq.a: Make sure she signs up for Part B during her seven-month window around 65, unless she has coverage from a current job (hers or a spouse's). The Part B penalty is 10% of the standard premium for each full year she could have enrolled but did not, and it usually lasts for life. NJ SHIP at 1-800-792-8820 can help for free.

faq.q: At what age do required minimum distributions start?
faq.a: Under current federal law, at 73. The first one can be delayed until April 1 of the following year. Roth IRAs have no required withdrawals while the owner is alive.

faq.q: How do I check if my dad's financial adviser is legitimate in New Jersey?
faq.a: Search the person and firm on FINRA BrokerCheck and the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure site. You can also call the New Jersey Bureau of Securities at 1-866-446-8378 (973-504-3600 from outside New Jersey).

faq.q: Does New Jersey tax Social Security?
faq.a: No. New Jersey does not tax Social Security benefits. Pensions and IRA withdrawals are taxable, but many people 62 and older can exclude them through the state's retirement income exclusion.

faq.q: Where can we get free retirement advice in New Jersey?
faq.a: NJ SHIP gives free Medicare counseling at 1-800-792-8820. AARP Foundation Tax-Aide prepares taxes for free at 1-888-227-7669. The New Jersey Bureau of Securities can tell you whether an adviser is registered.

title: Retiring with a New Jersey state pension: PERS, TPAF and PFRS
dek: How to apply through MBOS, what your tier means, the nine PERS and TPAF payment options, keeping state retiree health coverage with Medicare, and the rules on going back to work.
keyFacts: Apply online through MBOS no more than one year ahead; four to six months is recommended
PERS and TPAF service retirement: age 60 (Tiers 1 and 2), 62 (Tiers 3 and 4), 65 (Tier 5)
Your payment option cannot be changed once the pension becomes due and payable
Retiree health coverage requires Medicare Parts A and B once you are eligible
Division of Pensions and Benefits: 609-292-7524
body:
If your mom or dad worked for the State, a school district, a town or a county in New Jersey, their pension most likely comes from the Public Employees' Retirement System (PERS), the Teachers' Pension and Annuity Fund (TPAF) or the Police and Firemen's Retirement System (PFRS), all run by the NJ Division of Pensions and Benefits. You apply for retirement online through the Division's Member Benefits Online System, called MBOS. Paper applications are not accepted.

The Division recommends filing four to six months before your retirement date, and it will not take an application more than one year ahead. Your tier and years of service decide when you can retire and how much you get. At 65, keeping state retiree health coverage depends on signing up for Medicare Parts A and B. This guide is general information, not legal or financial advice. For your own numbers, call the Division at 609-292-7524.

How do I apply for a New Jersey state pension?

You apply online through MBOS on the Division's website, no more than one year before your retirement date. Filing four to six months ahead is recommended, and the Division must receive your application before your retirement date.

Every retirement starts on the first of a month, and never before the Division receives the application, so a late filing costs real money.

  1. Six to eight months out, get an estimate. Members within two years of retirement can run one in MBOS using the salary and service on file.
  2. Four to six months out, file online. Log in to MBOS and submit the retirement application. Have your bank routing and account numbers ready, because direct deposit is required and the application will not be processed without it.
  3. Send proof of age. A birth certificate with a visible seal, a passport or a current digital NJ driver's license or non-driver ID all work. Upload it in MBOS or mail a photocopy.
  4. Finish the paperwork within 90 days. All required forms must reach the Division within 90 days of your application, or it may be canceled and you would have to file again for a later date.
  5. Watch your mail. About three months out comes the retiree health offer. About a month out, the Board of Trustees votes on your retirement.

Your first check cannot be issued until 30 days after your retirement date or 30 days after board approval, whichever is later. Checks are dated the first of the month for the month before, and late approvals are paid back to your retirement date. You can change your date or option, or cancel, up to 30 days after your retirement date or board approval, whichever is later.

When can I retire, and what are the tiers?

For PERS and TPAF, your tier is set by when you enrolled. Tiers 1 and 2 can take a service retirement at 60, Tiers 3 and 4 at 62, and Tier 5 at 65. PFRS members can take a service retirement at 55 and must retire at 65, with limited exceptions.

PERS or TPAF tierEnrolledService retirement age
Tier 1Before July 1, 200760
Tier 2July 1, 2007 to November 1, 200860
Tier 3November 2, 2008 to May 21, 201062
Tier 4May 22, 2010 to June 27, 201162
Tier 5June 28, 2011 or later65

For Tiers 1 to 3, the yearly maximum pension is years of service divided by 55, times your average salary over your last (or highest) three years. For Tiers 4 and 5, it is years divided by 60, times the average of five years. A Tier 1 member with 22 years gets 22/55, or 40% of final average salary. Overtime does not count.

Early, veteran and deferred retirement

  • Early: 25 years of service before the tier's retirement age (30 years before 65 for Tier 5), with a reduced pension that depends on your tier and age. Tier 1 members retiring between 55 and 60 have no reduction.
  • Veteran: qualified veterans can retire at 60 with 20 years, or at 55 with 25 years.
  • Deferred: leave with 10 to 24 years before the tier's age, and file for a pension that starts at that age. File before you reach it, or your only choice becomes the Maximum Option.

Police and fire (PFRS)

PFRS service retirement is open at 55 with no minimum service. Special retirement is open at any age with 25 years and pays 65% of final compensation for Tiers 1 and 2 (60% for Tier 3), plus 1% a year beyond 25, up to 30 years. A 2023 law allows retirement at 20 years for members in PFRS before April 19, 2021, who retire by May 1, 2029. A member who has not filed by 65 is retired automatically, but no pension is paid until the application is in.

Which pension option should I choose?

PERS and TPAF members pick one of nine ways to be paid. The Maximum Option pays the most but stops at your death. The others pay you less so someone can keep getting money after you die. Once the first check is issued, you generally cannot change the option.

OptionWhat your beneficiary gets
MaximumNo monthly pension. Unpaid contributions plus interest, if any are left
A, B, C, D100%, 75%, 50% or 25% of your pension for life. If they die first, yours goes up to the Maximum
1A lump sum of whatever is left of your retirement reserve
2, 3100% or 50% for life. If they die first, yours stays reduced
4An amount you choose, up to your own pension, for life

Under Options A to D and 2 to 4, the beneficiary must be a person, and the younger that person is, the bigger the cut to your own check. Those beneficiaries can never be changed after retirement. Option 1 allows several beneficiaries, including a charity or your estate, and you can change them any time.

Group life insurance is separate from the pension option. Members with at least 10 years keep a reduced amount in retirement. You have 31 days after your job ends to convert the difference to an individual policy with Prudential, at 1-855-364-7783, without a medical exam.

The option choice is the one decision you cannot undo once the checks start.

PFRS works differently. It has no menu of options. When a retired PFRS member dies, a surviving spouse or partner receives a pension of 50% of final compensation, with added amounts for eligible children.

What happens to my health insurance when I retire?

If you have State Health Benefits Program (SHBP) or School Employees' Health Benefits Program (SEHBP) coverage at work, you will be offered retiree coverage if you are eligible. At 65, you must be enrolled in Medicare Part A and Part B to keep it.

Some people are enrolled automatically. Others must enroll online through Benefitsolver at mynjbenefitshub.nj.gov, and the offer letter says which applies. Some employers pay part or all of the cost for retirees with 25 or more years. Ask what you will pay.

The Medicare rules that trip people up

  • Parts A and B are required. If you or a covered spouse is 65, or has been on Social Security disability for 24 months, both must have Medicare A and B. Skip it and your SHBP or SEHBP coverage is terminated. Apply with Social Security 90 days before retiree coverage starts.
  • Two kinds of plans. Medicare retirees choose an Aetna Medicare Advantage plan or a Horizon Medicare supplement plan. Either way, a doctor who does not accept Medicare is not covered.
  • Drug coverage is automatic. Retirees on Medicare are enrolled in the OptumRx Medicare Part D plan. If you join another Part D plan, you lose the program's drug coverage. If you are in the Aetna Advantage plan and waive drugs for an individual Part D plan, your medical plan will be terminated.
  • Part B reimbursement varies. Some retirees get their Part B premium paid back, in full or capped, and others get nothing, depending on the employer, the contract and when they reached 25 years. Ask before you assume.

Our Medicare at 65 guide explains the sign-up windows. Keep paying Part B, because a lapse can end your state retiree coverage.

Can I work again after retiring from a New Jersey public job?

Yes, with limits. Private, federal and out-of-state jobs do not affect a regular service pension. Going back to a New Jersey public employer is where the rules bite.

  • Same employer: you need a complete break of at least 180 days from your retirement date (90 days for PFRS). Part-time, contract or consultant work during that window breaks the rule, and so can volunteering.
  • No deals in advance: any arrangement made before retirement to come back, in any role, can void the retirement and force you to repay every check.
  • A different public employer: wait at least 30 days after your retirement date or after board approval, whichever is later, before agreeing to a job not covered by your system.
  • Full-time in your old system: if you take a full-time job covered by your former system, you will generally be re-enrolled and your pension and retiree health coverage stop while you work.

A PERS or TPAF disability pension can be reduced by earnings from any job. If you are unsure about a job, the Division says to have the employer contact it before you accept. Our guide to working after 60 covers jobs, training and the Social Security earnings test.

How is a New Jersey public pension taxed?

Your pension is subject to federal income tax, except for accidental disability and accidental death benefits. New Jersey generally does not tax it until you have recovered your own contributions, and at 62 or older you may be able to exclude much or all of it.

Under the three-year rule in the NJ-1040 instructions, most retirees owe no New Jersey tax on the pension until the payments equal what they paid in. Retirees 62 or older, or disabled under Social Security rules, can use New Jersey's pension exclusion. The Division's April 2026 tax fact sheet lists a full exclusion of up to $100,000 for married couples filing jointly, $75,000 for single filers and $50,000 for married filing separately, if gross income is $100,000 or less. Partial exclusions apply up to $150,000. Our guide to how New Jersey taxes retirement income covers the details.

  • Withholding: federal tax is withheld at Single by default. New Jersey tax is withheld only if you ask, at least $10 a month. Change either in MBOS.
  • Moving away: if you live outside New Jersey, you do not owe New Jersey income tax on this pension.

For budgeting, under a 2011 law, Chapter 78, cost-of-living adjustments are suspended for all current and future retirees of every state-run system. Plan on the same monthly pension year after year. Our retirement planning checklist covers the rest of the budget, and free help with tax returns is in our free tax help guide.

How do I help a parent with their state pension?

Help your parent register in MBOS, which shows their account, beneficiaries and tax forms. Have their pension number or the last four digits of their Social Security number when you call. For their protection, the Division will not accept or confirm beneficiary changes over the phone or by email. Someone holding a legal power of attorney can apply for retirement for a member and choose a pension option. To name group life insurance beneficiaries, the document must specifically grant that power, so read the Division's options fact sheet before relying on one. Our estate planning guide explains powers of attorney.

When a retiree dies, call the Division promptly so payments stop and survivor or life insurance benefits can start. Our guide to what to do when a parent dies lists the other calls to make.

RelayDial 711, then 609-292-6683
Emailpensions.nj@treas.nj.gov
MailP.O. Box 295, Trenton, NJ 08625-0295

faq.q: How far ahead should I apply for my NJ pension?
faq.a: The Division of Pensions and Benefits recommends filing four to six months before your retirement date. You cannot file more than one year ahead, and the application must be received before your retirement date. You apply online through MBOS.

faq.q: What age can I retire with a PERS or TPAF pension?
faq.a: Service retirement is available at 60 for Tiers 1 and 2, at 62 for Tiers 3 and 4, and at 65 for Tier 5. Early retirement with a reduced pension is possible with 25 years of service (30 years for Tier 5).

faq.q: How do I help my mom apply for her teacher's pension?
faq.a: Help her register for MBOS on the Division's website, gather proof of age and her bank details for direct deposit, and file four to six months ahead. Someone with a legal power of attorney can apply for her. Read the Division's options fact sheet first. Call 609-292-7524 with questions.

faq.q: Do I have to sign up for Medicare to keep my state retiree health plan?
faq.a: Yes. Retirees and covered spouses who are eligible for Medicare must be enrolled in both Part A and Part B to stay in the SHBP or SEHBP. Coverage is terminated if an eligible person does not enroll.

faq.q: Can my dad go back to work part time at his old town job after retiring?
faq.a: Not right away. PERS retirees need a complete break of at least 180 days from their former employer (90 days for PFRS), and any job arranged before retirement can make the retirement invalid. Part-time work during that window counts as a violation. Have the employer contact the Division first.

faq.q: Do New Jersey state pensions get cost-of-living raises?
faq.a: Not currently. Under Chapter 78 of 2011, cost-of-living adjustments are suspended for all current and future retirees of the state-administered retirement systems.

title: Medigap plans in New Jersey: costs, enrollment and switching
dek: Which Medigap letters are sold in New Jersey, what they cost on the state's 2026 rate chart, how companies raise prices, and how to switch plans or add Part D without losing coverage.
keyFacts: Plans with the same letter have the same benefits; only the price differs
Your 6-month Medigap Open Enrollment Period starts when you are 65 and have Part B
Sept. 2026 NJ chart, woman at 65: Plan G about $148 to $261 a month
Plans C and F are closed to people new to Medicare since January 1, 2020
Free NJ SHIP counseling: 1-800-792-8820
body:
A Medigap policy, also called Medicare Supplement Insurance, pays some or all of the bills Original Medicare leaves behind, like the 20% coinsurance on doctor visits and the hospital deductible. In New Jersey, as in most states, the plans are standardized by letter. A Plan G from one company covers exactly what a Plan G from another company covers. Only the price is different, and in New Jersey those prices vary a lot.

Your best time to buy is the six months after you are 65 and enrolled in Part B. During that window no company can turn you down or charge more for your health. After it, they can. Medigap does not cover prescriptions, so most people also need a separate Part D drug plan. This guide covers which plans are sold here, what they cost, how prices rise and how to switch. If you are still choosing between Medigap and a Medicare Advantage plan, start with our Advantage vs. Medigap guide.

Which Medigap plans can I buy in New Jersey?

Plans are named by letter. On the September 2026 New Jersey rate chart for people turning 65, companies offered Plans A, B, D, G, a high-deductible Plan G, K, L, M and N. Plans C and F are closed to anyone new to Medicare on or after January 1, 2020.

Every company that sells Medigap must offer at least Plan A. Not every company sells every letter. On the state chart, Plan A, Plan G and Plan N were offered by almost every company. Plans B, K, L and M were offered by only a few.

PlanWhat it does
ABasic benefits only. Pays Part B coinsurance and Part A hospital coinsurance. Covers neither deductible
GPays everything Plan F did except the yearly Part B deductible ($283 in 2026)
High-deductible GSame as G after you pay $2,950 (2026) yourself
NLike G, but you pay up to $20 at some office visits and up to $50 at the ER if not admitted. Does not cover Part B excess charges
DLike G, but does not cover Part B excess charges
K and LPay 50% or 75% of most gaps, with a yearly cap of $8,000 (K) or $4,000 (L) in 2026

A Part B excess charge is the difference when a doctor is legally allowed to charge more than the Medicare-approved amount. Plan G covers excess charges. Plans D and N do not. If your mom sees specialists who bill this way, ask before you pick N.

If your parent already has Plan C or Plan F, or an older plan such as E, H, I or J, they can generally keep it. People who were eligible for Medicare before 2020 but did not enroll may still be able to buy C or F. Policies bought before June 1, 2010 may cover things newer policies do not, so think hard before dropping one.

How much does Medigap cost in New Jersey?

On the state's September 2026 chart for a 65-year-old woman buying in her open enrollment window, Plan G ran from about $148 to $261 a month, and Plan N from about $108 to $202, depending on the company. That is on top of the 2026 Part B premium of $202.90 and any Part D premium.

NJ SHIP, the state's free Medicare counseling program, publishes these charts. They list each company's monthly premium for every plan letter at age 65, with separate charts for women and men. If you are older than 65, the chart says to call the companies for a quote. The chart's rates apply when you buy in your open enrollment window or with a guaranteed issue right.

Sept. 2026 chart, woman at 65Monthly premium range
Plan G$147.88 to $260.98
Plan N$107.91 to $202.00

Other cost points to ask about:

  • Application fees. NJ SHIP notes some companies charge a one-time fee, such as $20 or $25, and some charge a fee for paying by credit card.
  • Discounts. Some companies offer household discounts for more than one policy, or discounts for automatic payments.
  • One policy per person. A Medigap policy covers one person. Married couples each buy their own.

Prices can differ by ZIP code for some companies. One insurer on the 2026 chart charged a different rate in certain Newark ZIP codes. Our county guide explains what does and does not change with your address.

Same letter, same benefits. Compare Plan G to Plan G, and let price and rate history decide.

How do Medigap companies set and raise prices?

Each company picks one of three pricing methods: community-rated, issue-age-rated or attained-age-rated. The method decides if your premium climbs just because you get older, so ask which one a policy uses before you buy.

  • Community-rated (no-age-rated). Generally everyone pays the same premium, whatever their age.
  • Issue-age-rated. The premium is based on your age when you buy. It will not rise because you get older.
  • Attained-age-rated. The premium is based on your current age and goes up as you age. It can be the cheapest at 65 and among the most expensive later.

Under all three methods, premiums can still rise for inflation and other reasons. In New Jersey, NJ SHIP notes that rate increases can come at any time during the year with approval from the NJ Department of Banking and Insurance (DOBI). That is why a low starting price is only half the question. Ask each company how often it has raised rates on the plan in recent years.

Your policy cannot be canceled because of your health. Any standardized Medigap policy bought after 1992 is guaranteed renewable. The company can drop you only if you stop paying, were not truthful on the application, or the company goes out of business.

When is the best time to buy Medigap?

During your six-month Medigap Open Enrollment Period. It starts the first month you have Part B and are 65 or older, and it happens only once. In that window you can buy any plan sold in New Jersey, and the company cannot charge more or say no because of your health.

After the window closes, New Jersey companies can ask health questions and can turn you down or charge more, unless you have a guaranteed issue right. The fall Medicare Open Enrollment Period does not reopen Medigap. Our Advantage vs. Medigap guide covers the guaranteed issue rights, the one-year trial right and New Jersey's rules for people under 65 who are on Medicare because of a disability.

Even in your open enrollment window, a company can make you wait up to six months before covering a condition that was diagnosed or treated in the six months before your policy starts. That wait is shortened or dropped if you had other health coverage, called creditable coverage, with no break longer than 63 days.

Still working at 65?

If you or your spouse has health coverage from a current job, you may be able to wait on Part B. Your Medigap window does not start until Part B does. Signing up for Part B early just to buy Medigap can waste your one window. See our Medicare at 65 guide before deciding.

Can I switch Medigap plans later?

Yes, you can apply for a different Medigap policy at any time of year. Outside your open enrollment window or a guaranteed issue situation, though, the new company can use your health history to say no.

  1. Compare first. Use the newest NJ SHIP chart and call companies for a quote at your current age.
  2. Apply and wait for approval. Do not cancel your current policy yet. On the application you will promise to cancel the old one.
  3. Use the free look period. Once you get the new policy, you have 30 days to decide whether to keep it. You pay both premiums for the month you have both.
  4. Then cancel the old policy. Call the old company and get the cancellation in writing. Once canceled, you cannot get it back.

If you have had your current policy for less than six months, the new one may make you wait for pre-existing conditions, minus the months you already had. If you are moving from Medigap to a Medicare Advantage plan, remember that Medigap cannot pay any Advantage costs, and coming back later may not be possible. Companies generally cannot sell you a Medigap policy while you are in an Advantage plan or have Medicaid.

Do I need a Part D drug plan with Medigap?

Usually yes. Medigap policies sold after 2005 do not cover prescriptions. Without Part D or other creditable drug coverage, you may owe a late enrollment penalty for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage.

The penalty is 1% of the national base premium ($38.99 in 2026) for every full month you went without coverage after your first chance to enroll. Wait 14 months and you pay 14% more, every month, for good. People who get Extra Help do not pay it. You can change Part D plans each year from October 15 to December 7.

In 2026, Part D caps what you pay for covered drugs at $2,100 for the year. In 2027 the cap rises to $2,400, and the highest deductible a plan can charge goes from $615 to $700. If prescriptions or premiums are a strain, New Jersey's PAAD program and the Medicare Savings Programs may help with drug and Part B costs.

Where can I get free help or make a complaint?

NJ SHIP gives free, unbiased Medicare counseling in all 21 counties. Counselors do not sell insurance. They can walk you through the rate charts and the rules for your situation.

WhoForPhone
NJ SHIPFree counseling, rate charts1-800-792-8820
NJ DOBIQuestions and complaints about a policy or company1-800-446-7467
MedicarePlan Finder, Part D1-800-633-4227

The DOBI consumer hotline is open 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday to Friday. Medicare's TTY line is 1-877-486-2048.

If you are helping a parent

  • Find out exactly when their Part B started, and whether they are still inside six months.
  • Write down their plan letter and current premium from the latest bill.
  • Never let a caller or visitor rush them into dropping a policy. Ask for any offer in writing and check it with NJ SHIP first. Our scams guide lists the warning signs.
  • Book a free NJ SHIP appointment and bring the list of prescriptions and doctors.

This is general information, not legal or insurance advice, and we do not recommend any company. Premiums change, so confirm every price with the company.

faq.q: What is the most popular Medigap plan in New Jersey?
faq.a: We could not find official enrollment numbers by plan for New Jersey. On the state's September 2026 rate chart, Plans A, G and N were offered by almost every company. Plans C and F are closed to people new to Medicare since 2020.

faq.q: How much is Medigap Plan G in NJ?
faq.a: On NJ SHIP's September 2026 chart for a 65-year-old woman, Plan G ranged from $147.88 to $260.98 a month depending on the company. Rates for men and for older buyers differ, so ask each company for a quote.

faq.q: Can I change Medigap plans anytime in New Jersey?
faq.a: You can apply any time of year, but outside your first six months on Part B or a guaranteed issue situation, the company can ask health questions and turn you down.

faq.q: How do I compare Medigap prices for my mom?
faq.a: Download NJ SHIP's current Medigap rate chart, compare the same plan letter across companies, then call companies for a quote at her age. Ask how each one sets its price and how often it has raised rates. NJ SHIP counselors at 1-800-792-8820 can help for free.

faq.q: Does Medigap cover prescriptions?
faq.a: No. Medigap policies sold after 2005 do not include drug coverage. You need a separate Part D plan or other creditable coverage to avoid a late enrollment penalty.

faq.q: Who do I call with a complaint about my dad's Medigap company?
faq.a: Call the NJ Department of Banking and Insurance consumer hotline at 1-800-446-7467, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday to Friday.

title: Life insurance after 60 in NJ: final expense and lost policies
dek: What older adults can buy, what to watch for in no-exam policies, and how families find a parent's lost policy and get it paid.
keyFacts: NJ life insurers must pay within 60 days of proof of death
Overdue claim payments earn interest under N.J.S.A. 17B:25-11
Individual life policies in NJ include a 10-day free look
NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator is free; searches can take 90 business days
DOBI consumer hotline: 1-800-446-7467
body:
Older adults in New Jersey can still buy life insurance after 60. The choices narrow and the price rises with age. Policies sold to people in their 60s, 70s and 80s are usually term policies, whole life policies, or small "final expense" policies that skip the medical exam. Those no-exam policies often pay only a partial benefit if death comes in the first few years.

If a parent has died and you think there was a policy, you can search for it for free. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) runs a Life Insurance Policy Locator, and New Jersey's Unclaimed Property Administration holds insurance payouts nobody claimed. Once you find a policy, New Jersey law gives the insurer 60 days after it receives proof of death to pay. This page is general information, not legal or financial advice.

What kinds of life insurance can you buy after 60?

There are two broad families, term and cash value. Small final expense policies are usually a type of whole life sold with simple or no health questions.

The NAIC, the national group of state insurance regulators, describes term life as coverage for a set period. It pays your beneficiaries only if you die during that term. It is meant to be lower cost for a specific stretch of years. Some term policies can be renewed at the end without a new health check, but the premium can jump. Ask what renewal will cost and whether the right to renew ends at a certain age.

Cash value policies, such as whole life and universal life, can be kept as long as you need them. They build a savings or investment value that the owner can borrow against or draw from while alive.

Final expense or guaranteed issue policies are the ones advertised on daytime TV and in the mail. They usually have small face amounts meant to cover a funeral and final bills. Many ask few or no health questions. That ease comes with a catch, covered in the next section.

TypeHow longBuilds cash?
TermSet number of yearsNo
Whole or universalFor life, if paidYes
Final expenseFor life, if paidOften small

Before your mom or dad buys anything new, look at what they already have. A pension plan, a former employer's group life plan, or a union or veterans benefit may already pay something at death. Our guide to funeral costs and prepaid funerals in NJ explains another way to set money aside for a funeral, through a funeral trust or funeral insurance policy tied to a funeral home.

What is a graded death benefit, and why does it matter?

A graded death benefit means the policy pays little or nothing beyond a refund if the insured person dies in the first few years. The full face amount only kicks in after that waiting stretch.

State regulators describe these products as policies that "have no or a limited death benefit in the first few years of coverage." They are often sold without medical underwriting and are aimed at people over 50. You may see them called graded, limited or modified death benefit policies. The length of the reduced period and what is paid during it vary by company, so read the policy's first page and the benefit schedule closely.

Ask one question first. What does this policy pay if my dad dies in year one, year two and year three?

Say your dad, 78, sees an ad promising coverage with "no medical exam." He signs up and pays every month. If he dies during the graded period, his family may get back only the premiums paid, plus whatever extra the policy promises, and not the face amount. That can still be fine if the goal is long-term. It is a poor fit if the family is counting on that money soon.

A few more things to check before signing:

  • Total premiums. Add up the yearly premium over the years your parent may live, then compare that total with the face amount.
  • What happens if a payment is missed. Ask how long the grace period is and whether coverage ends.
  • The agent's license. Look up the agent on the NJ Department of Banking and Insurance (DOBI) Licensee Search.
  • The free look period. New Jersey requires individual life policies to include a 10-day free look. Your parent can review the delivered policy and return it within that window.

Be wary of anyone who calls or knocks with a "final expense" offer and pushes for a signature today. Our guide to scams targeting NJ seniors covers pressure tactics and how to shut them down.

How do I find my parent's lost life insurance policy?

Start with their papers and bank records, then use two free searches, the NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator and New Jersey's unclaimed property search. Neither charges a fee.

  1. Go through paperwork and mail. Look for policy documents, premium notices, annual statements, and envelopes from insurers. Check a safe deposit box, desk drawers and the folder with the will. Our list of important papers shows what to gather.
  2. Read old bank and credit card statements. A regular payment to an insurance company is a strong clue. So is a deposit of dividends from one.
  3. Call past employers and unions. Ask the human resources or benefits office about group life coverage, including any coverage that continued into retirement.
  4. Use the NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator. It is free at naic.org, under Consumer, then Tools. You enter your name, mailing address and email, then your parent's Social Security number, legal first and last name, date of birth and date of death from the death certificate, plus veteran status and your relationship.
  5. Search New Jersey unclaimed property. The state holds insurance payouts that were never claimed. Search at unclaimedfunds.nj.gov. Our guide to finding unclaimed money in New Jersey walks through claims for a deceased parent.

A few things to know about the NAIC locator. Participating insurers check requests through a secure portal. You get a confirmation email. If a company finds a policy and you are the beneficiary, the company contacts you directly. If nothing is found, or you are not the beneficiary, you will not hear back. The NAIC says a search may take 90 business days or more. The tool only works for people who have died.

The locator works. The NAIC reported in September 2026 that insurers had found more than 780,000 matches worth nearly $17 billion since the tool started in 2016.

Watch out for paid "policy finders"

You do not need to pay anyone to run these searches. The NAIC locator is free, and New Jersey's Unclaimed Property Administration says it never charges a fee to search and claim.

How do you file a life insurance claim in New Jersey?

Call the insurer's claims line, ask for a claim form, and send it with a certified death certificate. In New Jersey, the company must pay within 60 days after it receives proof of death and anything else the policy lets it ask for.

  1. Get certified death certificates. Order several. Insurers, banks and pension plans each want one. Our guide to death certificates in NJ explains how to order them.
  2. Find the policy number and the insurer's full name. If you only have a company name that has since changed, the NAIC has a separate company lookup on its site.
  3. Call the claims department. Ask for the claim form, the list of documents they need, and the payout choices. Many policies allow a lump sum. Some offer other options.
  4. Send everything in a way you can track. Keep copies and write down the date it arrived.
  5. Follow up in writing. If the company needs more time, it must tell you why in writing.

Here is what New Jersey law (N.J.S.A. 17B:25-11) sets for individual life policies.

StepDeadline
Pay the claim60 days after proof
Notice of review or denial45 days, in writing
Decide after more papers90 days
Late paymentEarns interest

The days count from when the insurer receives proof of death, proof of the claimant's interest, and any other document it asked for under the policy. If a company tells you it is investigating, it must give a reason, except in some suspected fraud cases. Any part of the claim that is not in dispute still has to be paid on the 60-day clock.

Many families are handling the policy at the same time as the funeral, the bank and the house. Our checklist for what to do when a parent dies in New Jersey puts the life insurance call in order with everything else.

Should my parent sell a life insurance policy for cash?

Sometimes it helps, but DOBI urges caution. Selling a policy, called a viatical or life settlement, gives cash now and hands the death benefit to a stranger. Check the other options first.

In a life settlement, the owner sells the policy to a third party. The buyer becomes the new owner, pays the future premiums, and collects the death benefit later. New Jersey regulates these sales under the Viatical Settlements Act (N.J.S.A. 17B:30B), and providers and brokers must be licensed or registered with DOBI.

DOBI lists reasons a family might think twice. The policy may be worth more over time. Your parent will have to share private health and money details with strangers. And the payout will go to someone with no tie to your family. Before selling, DOBI suggests these steps:

  • Find out whether the policy has cash value your parent can borrow against.
  • Check for an accelerated death benefit, which can pay part of the benefit early, usually after a terminal illness diagnosis.
  • Ask the current insurer whether it would make a better offer.
  • Get several real bids from competing buyers.
  • Talk with a tax adviser and an unbiased financial professional.
  • Check how the cash could affect public benefits. DOBI names food stamps (SNAP), and money from a sale can also count against Medicaid limits.

That last point matters if your parent may need long-term care. Our guide to NJ FamilyCare and MLTSS explains how Medicaid looks at assets, and an elder law attorney can review the timing.

Where can we get help or file a complaint?

The New Jersey Department of Banking and Insurance handles questions and complaints about life insurers and agents. Call 1-800-446-7467 or 609-292-7272, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.

You can also file a complaint online through the DOBI consumer page. Include the policy number, the claim number, copies of letters, and a short timeline. DOBI can check whether a company followed the policy and state law. It cannot act as your lawyer or a court.

If you suspect insurance fraud, such as someone using your parent's name or a fake policy, call the NJ Office of the Insurance Fraud Prosecutor at 1-877-553-7283 (1-877-55-FRAUD).

Keep a simple insurance sheet

List each policy, the company, the policy number, the beneficiary and where the paperwork is kept. Store it with the will. It saves your family weeks of searching later. Our guide to estate planning in NJ covers beneficiary forms and the rest of the paperwork.

faq.q: How do I find out if my mom had life insurance after she died?
faq.a: Check her papers, mail and bank statements for premium payments, and call past employers about group coverage. Then submit a free request through the NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator at naic.org and search New Jersey unclaimed property at unclaimedfunds.nj.gov. If a company finds a policy and you are the beneficiary, it contacts you.

faq.q: How long does a life insurance company have to pay a claim in New Jersey?
faq.a: Under N.J.S.A. 17B:25-11, the insurer must pay within 60 days after it receives proof of death and any other documents the policy allows it to request. If it needs to investigate or denies the claim, it must tell you in writing within 45 days. Overdue payments earn interest.

faq.q: What is a graded death benefit?
faq.a: It is a feature of many no-exam and final expense policies. If the insured person dies in the first few years, the policy pays a reduced amount or no death benefit, and only pays the full face amount after that period. Ask exactly what is paid in each early year before buying.

faq.q: Can my dad cancel a life insurance policy he just bought?
faq.a: New Jersey requires individual life policies to include a 10-day free look period. He can review the policy after it is delivered and return it within that window. Check the policy's first page for the exact terms.

faq.q: Is it a good idea for my parent to sell a life insurance policy?
faq.a: It can bring cash, but DOBI urges caution. First check for cash value, an accelerated death benefit and an offer from the current insurer, get several bids, and talk with a tax adviser. Life settlement providers must be licensed or registered with DOBI.

title: Homeowners and flood insurance for older NJ homeowners
dek: What a standard policy covers, why flood needs its own policy, the FAIR Plan as a last resort, and what to do when a parent's house sits empty.
keyFacts: Standard NJ homeowners policies exclude flood
New NFIP flood policies usually take 30 days to start
NFIP home limits: $250,000 building, $100,000 contents
NJ FAIR Plan (NJIUA): 973-622-3838, last resort only
DOBI consumer hotline: 1-800-446-7467
body:
A standard homeowners policy in New Jersey covers the house, other structures like a shed or fence, your belongings, extra living costs after a covered loss, and liability if a visitor is hurt. It does not cover flood. Flood insurance is a separate policy, usually through the federal National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), and it generally takes 30 days to start.

For older homeowners and their families, the biggest risks are gaps nobody noticed. A policy that was never updated, no flood coverage on a house near a river, or a home left empty after a parent moves out. This guide covers what to check, where to turn if no company will write a policy, and how to file a claim. It is general information, not legal advice.

What does a standard homeowners policy cover?

Most policies have six parts, labeled Coverage A through F. Dwelling coverage is usually the anchor, and several other limits are set as a share of it.

The NJ Department of Banking and Insurance (DOBI) explains the parts this way in its Insuring Your Home guide.

PartWhat it covers
A. DwellingThe house and built-in systems
B. Other structuresSheds, fences, often 10% of A
C. BelongingsContents, often 50% of A
D. Loss of useLiving costs, often up to 20% of A
E. LiabilityInjuries to others, legal defense
F. Medical to othersGuests' bills, often $1,000 each

Replacement cost or actual cash value?

This one detail can change a claim check by thousands. Replacement cost is what it takes to repair or replace with similar materials at today's prices. Actual cash value is what the item is worth now, after age and wear. DOBI says homes are typically insured at replacement cost, while belongings are often paid at actual cash value unless you add a replacement cost endorsement.

Say your mom has had the same policy for 30 years and the dwelling limit has barely moved. Rebuilding costs have climbed since then. Ask the agent whether the dwelling limit would still rebuild the house today.

What is usually left out

  • Flood. Excluded. Insurers must remind policyholders of this in writing at least once a year under a DOBI rule.
  • Earthquake and other earth movement.
  • Sewer backup and sump pump overflow. Excluded unless you add an endorsement, which DOBI says is usually limited to $5,000.
  • Wear and tear and neglect. A slow leak that rotted a floor over months is usually not covered.

Do older NJ homeowners need flood insurance?

Many do, even outside mapped flood zones. FEMA says that from 2014 to 2024, almost one third of NFIP claims came from areas outside high-risk zones.

NFIP policies are sold through insurance agents in communities that take part in the program. You buy building and contents coverage separately, each with its own deductible. FEMA lists residential limits of up to $250,000 for the structure and $100,000 for contents. If a home is in a high-risk Special Flood Hazard Area and has a mortgage from a federally regulated lender, flood insurance is required. Once the mortgage is paid off, no lender requires it, so it is easy to let it lapse without thinking.

The 30-day wait

A new NFIP policy usually takes effect 30 days after purchase. Buying when a storm is in the forecast is too late. The main exceptions are coverage bought with a new, increased, extended or renewed mortgage, added coverage chosen on a renewal bill, and a home newly mapped into a high-risk area if coverage is bought within 13 months of the map change.

How to check a parent's flood risk

The NJ Department of Environmental Protection runs a Flood Risk Notification Tool. Type in the address to see whether it sits in a FEMA Special or Moderate Flood Hazard Area. You can also ask the agent for a flood quote, which is based on the property's own risk.

New Jersey's flood risk notification law, enacted July 3, 2023, adds another layer. Since March 20, 2024, every seller must disclose whether the property is in one of those FEMA flood areas and any flood history they actually know about, before the buyer is bound by a contract. Landlords must tell prospective tenants the same kind of information. If your parent is selling, the questions are on the Seller's Property Condition Disclosure Statement. Our downsizing guide covers the rest of the sale.

If you are looking beyond NFIP, DOBI keeps a list of companies that write private flood coverage on its list of homeowners insurers. Being on the list is not an endorsement.

What if no company will insure the house?

Try several agents and companies first. If every regular insurer says no, New Jersey has a last-resort option, the New Jersey Insurance Underwriting Association, also called the FAIR Plan.

The FAIR Plan insures homes, mobile homes and rental units. DOBI says it gives basic property coverage, such as fire, lightning, wind and smoke. It does not include personal liability, and theft coverage is only an optional add-on. That means a FAIR Plan policy alone leaves your parent without protection if a visitor is hurt. Ask an agent about separate liability coverage.

A homeowner can apply to the FAIR Plan directly or through any licensed agent. Reach it at 973-622-3838 or njiua.org. DOBI advises using it only if you cannot get insurance anywhere else, including the surplus lines market that some agents use for harder-to-place homes.

Which discounts and deductibles should you ask about?

Ask about bundling, safety devices and long-time customer credits. Then look hard at the hurricane deductible, which can be far higher than the regular one.

DOBI lists these common discounts:

  • Home and auto with the same company
  • Smoke detectors, alarm systems and sprinklers
  • No one in the household smokes
  • Long-time policyholder
  • A higher regular deductible, which lowers the premium

Safety upgrades can do double duty. A monitored alarm or new smoke detectors protect a parent who lives alone and may earn a protective device credit. Our guide to aging in place in NJ covers home changes.

Hurricane and windstorm deductibles

Many New Jersey policies have a separate hurricane deductible, set as a percentage of the dwelling limit, often 1, 2, 5 or 10 percent. DOBI says it applies when the National Weather Service names a hurricane and sustained winds of 74 mph are measured anywhere in New Jersey. On a home insured for $200,000, a 2 percent deductible is $4,000. Find that number on the declarations page now, not after a storm.

Read the declarations page once a year. That is where the gaps hide.

What happens to coverage when a parent moves out or the house sits empty?

Call the insurer before the house is empty. Many policies limit or drop some coverage once a home is vacant or unoccupied for a set time, and the wording differs by company.

This comes up often. A parent moves in with family, goes to rehab, or moves to assisted living, and the house waits to be sold. Ask the insurer these questions in writing:

  • How does the policy define vacant and unoccupied, and after how many days do limits apply?
  • Which coverages shrink or stop, such as vandalism, broken pipes or theft?
  • Can we add a vacancy endorsement, or do we need a different policy?
  • What checks do you expect, such as heat on in winter and regular visits?

DOBI notes that an unoccupied home may be hard to insure with standard companies, which can push it to the surplus lines market. If your parent has a reverse mortgage, keeping insurance in force is part of the loan terms. Our reverse mortgage guide explains what happens after a move out.

Condos

A condo owner usually needs a unit owner's policy, often called an HO-6. The association's master policy covers the building and common areas. Your parent's policy picks up belongings, liability, and parts of the unit the master policy leaves out. Ask the association for its master policy summary and compare.

How do you file a homeowners claim, and what if it goes wrong?

Call the insurer or agent promptly, protect the house from more damage, and document everything. Keep every receipt, including hotel and meal costs if your parent cannot stay in the home.

  1. Report it. Call the police for theft. Then call the agent or company with the policy number ready.
  2. Make temporary repairs. Board a window or tarp a roof. DOBI says those costs are usually covered. Hold off on permanent repairs until the adjuster has seen the damage.
  3. Keep damaged items. Do not throw anything out until the insurer has inspected it.
  4. Send an itemized list. Include purchase dates, prices and replacement costs, with photos and receipts.
  5. Review the estimate. Go over it with your contractor and the adjuster before you accept.

A home inventory makes step four far easier. DOBI suggests going room by room, including the garage, basement and attic, with photos or video, and storing the list away from the house. Doing this with a parent is a good weekend project.

If there is a mortgage, the claim check may be made out to the lender too. The lender may release money in stages as repairs are done. Call the mortgage company and your bank as soon as the check arrives.

After a big storm, be careful with anyone who knocks offering repairs. Do not sign over a claim or pay a big deposit at the door. Our scams guide covers home repair scams.

Renewals, cancellations and complaints

DOBI explains that a company must mail or deliver a nonrenewal notice at least 30 days before the policy ends, with the specific reason. Higher rates or worse terms at renewal also need 30 days' written notice. There is no grace period for a late homeowners premium, so set up autopay or a reminder if a parent's bills are slipping.

For questions or complaints, call DOBI at 1-800-446-7467 or 609-292-7272, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., or file online at the DOBI consumer page. Include the policy and claim numbers and copies of letters. DOBI can check whether the company followed the policy and state law, but it cannot act as a court.

faq.q: Does homeowners insurance cover flooding in New Jersey?
faq.a: No. Standard homeowners policies exclude flood, and insurers must remind policyholders of that in writing each year. Flood coverage is a separate policy, usually through the National Flood Insurance Program, bought through an insurance agent.

faq.q: How long does it take for flood insurance to start?
faq.a: A new NFIP policy usually takes effect 30 days after purchase. Exceptions include coverage bought with a new, increased, extended or renewed mortgage, and coverage bought within 13 months after a home is newly mapped into a high-risk flood area.

faq.q: How do I check if my dad's house is in a flood zone?
faq.a: Enter the address in the NJ Department of Environmental Protection's Flood Risk Notification Tool, linked from dep.nj.gov/flooddisclosure. It shows whether the property is in a FEMA Special or Moderate Flood Hazard Area. An agent can also quote flood coverage based on the home's own risk.

faq.q: What should I do about insurance when my mom moves out and the house is empty?
faq.a: Call the insurer before the house is empty. Ask how the policy defines vacant and unoccupied, which coverages shrink after how many days, and whether you need a vacancy endorsement or another policy. Keep the heat on and check the house regularly.

faq.q: What if no insurance company will cover a house in NJ?
faq.a: Try several agents first. If every standard insurer refuses, the New Jersey Insurance Underwriting Association (FAIR Plan) offers basic property coverage. It does not include liability, and theft is optional. Call 973-622-3838 or visit njiua.org.

faq.q: Where do I complain about a homeowners insurance claim in NJ?
faq.a: Call the NJ Department of Banking and Insurance at 1-800-446-7467 or 609-292-7272, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., or file online at nj.gov/dobi/consumer.htm. Include your policy and claim numbers and copies of letters.

title: Car insurance for older drivers in New Jersey
dek: What New Jersey requires in 2026, why Medicare changes your PIP choice, the defensive driving discount, and what to do with the policy when a parent stops driving.
keyFacts: 2026 Standard Policy minimums: $35,000 per person, $70,000 per accident, $25,000 property damage
Medicare and Medicaid cannot be used for the PIP Health Care Primary option
NJ law requires insurers to offer a discount for an MVC-approved defensive driving course
Surrender the plates to the MVC before canceling insurance on a car you no longer use
DOBI Consumer Hotline: 1-800-446-7467
body:
Every car registered in New Jersey must be insured, and the state offers two kinds of policies. The Basic Policy meets the legal minimum at a lower price but leaves you exposed if you hurt someone. The Standard Policy is what most New Jersey drivers choose. For policies issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2026, its lowest liability limits are $35,000 per person and $70,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage.

Older drivers face a few choices that matter more after 65. Medicare cannot be used as your primary coverage for car accident injuries. A state-approved defensive driving course earns an insurance discount that New Jersey law requires insurers to offer. And when a parent stops driving, the order in which you cancel things matters. This guide covers all of it. It is general information, not legal advice, and we do not recommend any insurer.

What car insurance does New Jersey require?

At minimum, a Basic Policy. Most drivers who own a home or have savings buy the Standard Policy, which offers much higher liability protection.

The New Jersey Department of Banking and Insurance (DOBI) sets out the two options side by side. Here are the main differences, using DOBI's 2026 figures.

CoverageStandardBasic
Injury liabilityFrom $35,000 per person and $70,000 per accidentNot included. $10,000 optional
Property damageFrom $25,000$5,000
Medical (PIP)$15,000 to $250,000 or more$15,000
Uninsured motoristIncludedNone
Right to sueYour choiceLimited only

The liability minimums went up in two steps under a 2022 state law. The second step took effect January 1, 2026. If your parent's old limits fell below the new floor, the insurer had to raise them at renewal and let them know. Check the declarations page if you are not sure what your mom or dad has now.

DOBI describes the Basic Policy as an option for people with few family responsibilities and few assets to protect. An older adult who owns a house, has retirement savings or a pension has a lot to protect. With no liability coverage, a driver who causes a crash may have to pay the injured person out of pocket, and the insurer will not provide a lawyer.

The right to sue choice

On a Standard Policy, you pick between the Unlimited Right to Sue and the Limited Right to Sue. The limited option costs less. It means you give up suing for pain and suffering unless the injury is on a specific list, such as a displaced fracture, significant scarring, loss of a body part, a permanent injury or death. It does not affect your medical bills, which PIP pays either way. The Basic Policy always carries the limited option.

A low-cost policy for Medicaid members

New Jersey also has a Special Automobile Insurance Policy for drivers enrolled in federal Medicaid with hospitalization. DOBI lists it at $365 a year. It covers medical care after an accident, not damage you cause to others. If your parent is on NJ FamilyCare, ask an agent or call DOBI at 1-800-446-7467 about it.

Can Medicare pay first for car accident injuries in NJ?

No. DOBI says Medicare and Medicaid cannot be used for the Health Care Primary option. If your parent is on Medicare, their auto policy's Personal Injury Protection (PIP) is the coverage that pays first.

PIP is New Jersey's no-fault medical coverage. It pays your own medical bills after a crash no matter who caused it. Younger drivers with employer health plans can lower their premium by naming their health insurer as primary. That shortcut is not available on Medicare, so the PIP limit your parent picks matters more.

On a Standard Policy, the usual PIP limit is $250,000 with a $250 deductible. You can save money by choosing a lower limit ($15,000, $50,000, $75,000 or $150,000) or a higher deductible ($500, $1,000, $2,000 or $2,500). Whatever deductible you choose, you also pay 20 percent of medical bills between the deductible and $5,000. Even at a lower limit, PIP pays up to $250,000 for certain catastrophic injuries, such as serious brain or spinal cord injuries.

On Medicare, PIP pays first. Pick the limit with that in mind.

Before trimming PIP, think about what a hospital stay and rehab could cost. If your parent still has a non-Medicare health plan, such as coverage through a working spouse, ask that plan in writing whether it covers auto accident injuries before choosing it as primary.

The extra PIP package

Standard policies offer extra PIP benefits for lost income, essential services and funeral expenses. Essential services pays for things you normally do yourself, like cleaning, laundry, mowing the lawn or shoveling snow, while you recover. For a retiree who lives alone, that benefit may matter more than lost wages. You can decline the package to save money, so ask what it costs on your parent's policy.

Does a defensive driving course lower car insurance in NJ?

Yes. DOBI says New Jersey law requires insurers to offer a discount to drivers who complete a defensive driving course approved by the Motor Vehicle Commission (MVC). The New Jersey Driver Manual calls it a multi-year discount.

The MVC keeps a list of approved classroom and online courses. It also lists mature driver courses designed for drivers 55 and older, which cover changes in vision, hearing, reaction time and flexibility. Our guide to driving later in life explains the two-point reduction on a driving record. Here is how to make sure the insurance savings actually show up.

  1. Pick a course from the MVC list. Only courses on the state's approved list count. Courses are listed on the MVC Driver Programs page.
  2. Call the insurer first. Ask how big the discount is, how long it lasts and what proof they need.
  3. Finish the course and keep the certificate. The provider reports completion to the MVC within 7 to 10 business days. Your insurer may still want its own copy.
  4. Check the next bill. If the discount is missing, send the certificate again and note the date you sent it.

Other discounts DOBI says to ask about include multiple cars on one policy, bundling with a homeowners policy, and safety features. Insurers must offer discounts for anti-lock brakes, air bags and anti-theft recovery systems.

Why did my parent's car insurance go up?

Rates depend on many things, some of them out of your control. DOBI lists age, where the car is kept, the car itself, how far it is driven, the driving record, claims history and, for some insurers, a credit-based insurance score.

New Jersey insurers sort drivers into rating tiers. Each company sets its own tier rules, so the same driver can get very different prices from different companies. That is why DOBI tells people to compare several insurers for the same coverage. You can shop at any time, not only at renewal. If you switch, never cancel the old policy until the new one is in effect.

A few protections are worth knowing:

  • Credit scores have limits. In New Jersey, an insurer cannot use an insurance score to deny, cancel or non-renew a policy. Insurance scoring models also cannot consider age.
  • Changes can bring refunds. You can change coverage at any time. If you lower limits or drop optional coverage, you are owed a refund of unused premium within 60 days.
  • Mid-term cancellation is rare. An insurer can cancel during the policy term only for fraud, a suspended license or unpaid premiums, and must send a 15-day notice first.
  • Driving less may count. Insurers ask for annual mileage when they price a policy. If your mom now drives only to the store and the doctor, tell the insurer.

Be wary of calls, texts or mailers promising cheap car insurance. Check that any agent or company is licensed through DOBI before paying anything, and see our scams guide for the warning signs.

What happens to the car insurance when a parent stops driving?

If the car stays registered, it must stay insured. Turn in the license plates to the MVC first, and only then cancel or change the insurance.

This order trips up a lot of families. New Jersey law requires every registered vehicle to be insured. When an insurer reports a dropped policy, the MVC can send a suspension notice to the registered owner. DOBI's guide says that if a car is off the road and the insurance lapses, the owner should surrender the plates so there is no uninsured registered vehicle. A lapse of more than 30 days can also push someone into the higher-priced assigned risk market later.

  1. Decide what happens to the car. Sell it, give it to a family member, donate it or keep it parked.
  2. Surrender the plates. Bring them to any MVC agency, hand them to staff or use the plate drop box, and keep the receipt.
  3. Then call the insurer. Cancel the policy or remove the car, and ask for any refund of unused premium.
  4. If a relative takes the car, they must register and insure it in their own name before driving it.

If your dad is still licensed but should not drive the family car, tell the insurer. Every licensed driver in a household must be disclosed. DOBI calls failure to do so a possible form of insurance fraud. A named driver exclusion can remove a driver from collision and comprehensive coverage on a specific car, which may lower the premium. But if that driver takes the car anyway and crashes, there is no collision or comprehensive coverage, so this only works if the keys are truly out of reach.

When the car goes, the trips don't have to. Our guide on when a parent stops driving covers the conversation and the first month. For getting around, see rides to medical appointments and NJ Transit reduced fares. A non-driver ID replaces the license for banking and travel.

What should my parent do after a car accident?

Report it to the insurer as soon as possible, even if it seemed minor. Get a copy of the police report and keep every receipt.

DOBI suggests writing down insurance details for every car involved, witness names and numbers, the officers' names and badge numbers, and how the crash happened. State rules require the insurer to contact you within 10 working days after you report a loss, or within 7 working days if it plans to inspect the car. The inspection must be at a reasonably convenient time and place. If a claim is denied, the insurer must explain why in writing.

After a crash, offer to sit in on the call with the insurer. Keep the policy, claim number and police report together. Our important papers checklist can help you keep the policy where you can find it.

Where can I get help or file a complaint about car insurance in NJ?

Call DOBI's Consumer Hotline at 1-800-446-7467 or 609-292-7272, or file a complaint online at dobi.nj.gov. DOBI cannot recommend an insurer, but it can look into how a company handled your parent's policy or claim.

  • Mail: NJ DOBI, Consumer Inquiry and Response Center, P.O. Box 471, Trenton, NJ 08625-0471.
  • Canceled policy: You can appeal a cancellation to DOBI, but keep shopping for coverage while you wait.
  • Claim disputes: DOBI's Office of Insurance Claims Ombudsman investigates and helps resolve claim complaints.
  • Can't find coverage: The Personal Automobile Insurance Plan, the state's assigned risk plan, can be reached through a producer. Call 1-800-652-2471 to find one.
  • Suspected fraud: Call the Office of Insurance Fraud Prosecutor at 1-877-55-FRAUD.
Before you call

Have the policy number, the declarations page, any letters from the insurer and a short timeline of what happened. If you are calling for a parent, the insurer may need your mom or dad on the line to give permission, or a copy of a power of attorney.

faq.q: What is the minimum car insurance in New Jersey in 2026?
faq.a: The Basic Policy is the legal minimum, with $5,000 in property damage liability and $15,000 in PIP medical coverage. The Standard Policy, which most drivers choose, starts at $35,000 per person and $70,000 per accident for injury liability and $25,000 for property damage on policies issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2026.

faq.q: My mom is on Medicare. Can she use it as primary for car accident injuries?
faq.a: No. The Department of Banking and Insurance says Medicare and Medicaid cannot be used for the Health Care Primary option. Her auto policy's PIP coverage pays first, so choose the PIP limit and deductible with that in mind.

faq.q: How do I get the defensive driving discount for my dad?
faq.a: Have him take a course from the Motor Vehicle Commission's approved list, including the mature driver courses for drivers 55 and older. Call the insurer first to ask how big the discount is and what proof it needs, then check the next bill.

faq.q: How do I cancel car insurance for my mom after she stops driving?
faq.a: Surrender the license plates at an MVC agency first and keep the receipt. Then call the insurer to cancel or remove the car. Canceling insurance on a car that is still registered can lead to a suspension notice from the MVC.

faq.q: Can an insurer cancel my parent's policy because of age or credit?
faq.a: New Jersey insurers cannot use an insurance score to deny, cancel or non-renew a policy, and scoring models cannot consider age. During the policy term, an insurer can cancel only for fraud, a suspended license or unpaid premiums, with a 15-day notice.

faq.q: Who do I call with a car insurance complaint in NJ?
faq.a: Call the Department of Banking and Insurance Consumer Hotline at 1-800-446-7467 or 609-292-7272, or file a complaint online at dobi.nj.gov.
