title: How to find unclaimed money in New Jersey
dek: Search New Jersey's unclaimed property list for free, claim money for yourself or a parent who died, and check the federal and insurance databases most families miss.
keyFacts: Search free at unclaimedfunds.nj.gov. The state never charges a fee
Unclaimed Property Administration: 609-292-9200
Heirs need Surrogate's Court papers dated within the past year
Finder deals signed within 24 months of the state receiving the money are void
The state pays interest when it returns your property
body:
New Jersey holds unclaimed money for residents and former residents, and searching for it is free. Go to the state's official site, unclaimedfunds.nj.gov, type in a last name, and file a claim online if something turns up. The New Jersey Unclaimed Property Administration (UPA), part of the state Treasury, says it never charges a fee to search or to claim.

Unclaimed property includes uncashed checks, forgotten bank accounts, insurance proceeds, stock and dividends, and refunds or credit balances. When a business loses touch with an owner for long enough, state law requires it to turn the money over to the state. The owner, or their heirs, never loses the right to it. This guide shows how to search, what the state will ask for, how to claim for a parent who has died, and where else to look. It is general information, not legal advice.

How do I search for unclaimed money in New Jersey?

Search by last name at unclaimedfunds.nj.gov, the UPA's free search site. If you see a listing at an address where you once lived, it is probably yours.

Some tips that make a search work better:

  • Try every name. Search maiden names, married names, nicknames and common misspellings. Search your parents, grandparents and any relative whose estate you handled.
  • Look at the address. New Jersey shows only the owner's name and reported address. It does not show the company or the amount. If the address is not one where the person lived or did business, the listing is probably someone else's.
  • Know what won't show. The site does not display amounts under $10. Money orders, cashier's checks and gift cards are often reported with no name at all.
  • Search other states. If your mom or dad ever lived or worked outside New Jersey, use MissingMoney.com, which the UPA links to for property held by other states.
  • Check the county lists. Each year the UPA publishes newly reported property in a statewide newspaper ad. The 2026 lists by county are posted on the UPA website.

If you can't find something you expected, the UPA has a Search Request form. Staff run a manual search and the state says to allow up to 2 weeks for an answer. Timing matters too. Companies report most property by October 31 each year, and the UPA says it can take up to 3 months to load new property into the search site. If a bank sent your parent a letter saying money would go to the state, it may not appear online right away.

The state never charges a fee to search for or claim unclaimed property.

How do I file a claim, and what will the state ask for?

File through the search site by choosing "Continue To File Claim." The UPA then emails you a list of any documents it needs, and you upload them online.

  1. Find the property and start the claim. Select each listing that belongs to you and pick the right claimant type, such as owner or heir.
  2. Enter the Social Security number. The UPA uses it to confirm ownership and to report interest. If you are claiming for someone else, enter the owner's number, not yours.
  3. Watch your email. Some claims are approved with no paperwork. Others get a claim form listing what to send.
  4. Send only what they ask for. The UPA asks people not to send documents until it requests them. Typical requests include a photo ID with a signature, proof of the Social Security number and proof of the old address.
  5. Track it. Check the status online with your claim ID.

Some property needs originals. A bearer bond or coupon must be the original, not a photocopy, and an old savings account may require the original passbook. Gift cards need the original card. If the property is stock, the state may have sold the shares after holding them for a year. In that case you receive the sale proceeds, as state law sets out.

Interest and taxes

The UPA pays interest from the date it received the property until your claim is approved. The property itself is not income, because it was already yours. If the interest is more than $10, you will get a 1099-INT form in January. If the claim included stock that was sold, you may get a 1099-B. Ask a tax preparer how to report them. Our free tax help guide lists free options.

The UPA office is not open to the public and cannot hand out checks in person. If the status says paid but no check arrived, wait at least 30 days from the issue date before asking for a new one.

How do I claim unclaimed money for my mom or dad who died?

You need legal authority to act for the estate. In practice that means documents from the county Surrogate's Court, dated within the past year, along with a copy of the death certificate.

The UPA lets someone claim property that is not in their own name only if they have a legal right to it, such as an executor or administrator of an estate. A power of attorney is not enough once the owner has died. The UPA says it will require probate documents in that case.

For a parent who lived in New Jersey at death, here is what the state typically asks for:

  • Probate papers. Proof from the Surrogate in the county where your parent lived that you can act for the estate, dated within one year.
  • Death certificate. Send a photocopy only. Our guide to death certificates in New Jersey explains how to order certified copies.
  • Your ID and Social Security proof. A photo ID with your signature, and a document showing your SSN as executor or administrator.
  • Your parent's Social Security number. Not needed separately if it appears on the death certificate.
  • Proof of your parent's old address. Something tying them to the address on the listing.

If both parents have died and the property was in both names, the UPA wants a death certificate for each, and a surrogate certificate for whoever died most recently. If your parent lived in another state, that state's probate rules apply.

Say your dad died two years ago in Morris County

The estate is settled, and your sister was executor. You find a $640 listing in his name at his old Parsippany address. Your sister files the claim as executor. Her surrogate certificate is now more than a year old, so she would need a fresh one from the Morris County Surrogate before the UPA will pay.

Estate questions can get tangled, especially with no will or several heirs. Our when a parent dies guide covers the Surrogate's Court and the first steps. An elder law attorney can help if heirs disagree.

Should I pay a company that offers to find my money?

You don't need to. Anything a finder can claim, you can claim yourself for free. New Jersey law also limits what finders can charge.

The UPA says heir finders and locators charge up to 20 percent of the property's value. Under New Jersey law (N.J.S.A. 46:30B-106), a finder agreement signed within 24 months after the property was turned over to the state is void and unenforceable. After that, the fee cannot exceed 20 percent, and the agreement must be in writing, signed by the owner, and must spell out what the property is, what it is worth and what the owner keeps after the fee. Agreements signed before the property was presumed abandoned are capped at 35 percent under the same rules.

If you get a letter from a finder, read it as a tip. Search unclaimedfunds.nj.gov yourself. If the money is there, file the claim directly and keep the whole amount.

Where else can I look for lost money?

State unclaimed property is only one source. Federal agencies and the insurance industry run their own free searches.

WhatWhere to look
Old company pensionPBGC unclaimed benefits search
401(k) or pensionDOL Retirement Savings Lost and Found
Life insuranceNAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator
Savings bondsTreasuryDirect, FS Form 1048
Tax refundIRS, Form 1310 for a deceased parent

Pensions and retirement plans

The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) holds benefits that were never paid when a private employer's plan ended. Search by last name and the last four digits of the Social Security number. PBGC updates the list quarterly. The Department of Labor's Retirement Savings Lost and Found database finds private employer and union plans tied to your Social Security number. You need an identity-verified Login.gov account, and you can search only your own number. To look for a plan that belonged to a spouse or parent who has died, contact the former employer or union. The Labor Department's Benefits Advisors can help you find them at 1-866-444-3272. Neither tool covers IRAs or government pensions.

Life insurance

The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) runs a free Life Insurance Policy Locator. You enter details from the death certificate, and participating insurers check for a match. The NAIC says searches can take 90 business days or more. You hear back only if a policy is found and you are the beneficiary or have legal authority. Our life insurance guide has more on finding a parent's policy and filing a claim.

Savings bonds and tax refunds

The Treasury retired its Treasury Hunt search tool on September 30, 2025. If you think a parent owned paper savings bonds that are lost, file FS Form 1048, the Treasury's claim form for lost, stolen or destroyed bonds. It is on the TreasuryDirect forms page. For a federal tax refund owed to a parent who died, a representative who was not appointed by a court files Form 1310 with the final return. A surviving spouse filing jointly or a court-appointed representative does not need it.

How do I spot an unclaimed money scam?

Real government offices don't charge to release your money. Anyone asking for a fee, a gift card or bank login to "unlock" a claim is running a scam.

  • Fees up front. The UPA never charges to search or claim. The Labor Department says it does not charge to recover funds either.
  • Requests for passwords or codes. The Labor Department says it will never ask for a password or one-time passcode, or ask to control your screen.
  • Look-alike websites. New Jersey's search is at unclaimedfunds.nj.gov. Type it yourself instead of clicking a link in a text or email.
  • Pressure. Unclaimed property in New Jersey does not expire. The state holds it until a valid claim is made, so there is no reason to rush.

If something feels off, call the UPA at 609-292-9200 before you share anything. Our scams guide covers other schemes aimed at older adults, and a yearly search fits well into retirement planning.

faq.q: Is it safe to search for unclaimed money in New Jersey?
faq.a: Yes, if you use the official site, unclaimedfunds.nj.gov. The Unclaimed Property Administration says searching and claiming are free. Type the address yourself instead of clicking links in texts or emails.

faq.q: How do I claim unclaimed money for my mom who passed away?
faq.a: Whoever has legal authority over her estate, usually the executor or administrator, files the claim. The state will ask for documents from the county Surrogate's Court dated within the past year, a photocopy of the death certificate, ID, and proof of her old address.

faq.q: How do I check if my dad has unclaimed money in other states?
faq.a: Search MissingMoney.com, which New Jersey's search site links to for property held by other states. Also search the state where he lived or worked if it is not listed there.

faq.q: How long does a New Jersey unclaimed property claim take?
faq.a: It varies. Some claims are approved with no paperwork. If you ask the state to run a manual search, allow up to 2 weeks for a reply. You can check your claim status online with your claim ID.

faq.q: Do I have to pay taxes on unclaimed money?
faq.a: The property itself is not income, according to the Unclaimed Property Administration. The interest the state pays is reportable, and you will get a 1099-INT if it is more than $10. Ask a tax preparer how to report it.

faq.q: Should I sign with a company that says it found money for me?
faq.a: You can claim it yourself for free. In New Jersey, a finder agreement signed within 24 months after the property went to the state is void, and later fees are capped at 20 percent.
